subtopic: SUGGESTED NATIONAL SURVEY OF EXTENT OF MENTAL ILLNESS
SUGGESTED NATIONAL SURVEY OF EXTENT OF MENTAL ILLNESS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of co-operating with the provincial authorities and such professional and other groups as may be interested, in

Mental Illness Survey
making a national survey of the extent of mental illness, its causes, problems and methods of treatment.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I make no apologies for introducing at this time a resolution on mental health. I am sure hon. members will appreciate that what I have to say will, of course, be the remarks, shall I say, of a simple layman. While I will try to sketch out the extent of various illnesses which are encompassed, generally speaking, within the general field of mental health or, as it is more formally called in professional circles, the field of psychiatry, I will not, nor could I, talk in specific terms of the symptoms of the variety of mental illnesses which are known to the medical profession.
What I hope to attain this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, is to create an awareness among hon. members of this house and among the Canadian people of the need for effective action. In a democratic society we are often slow in facing up to problems to which, though serious, we fail to attach any real sense of urgency. Consider, for example, our refusal to believe that Hitler would plunge the world into war and again our slowness in adopting measures to provide for social benefits. We do not act this way through any malice but merely through a social habit of refusing to react promptly in relation to matters we consider unpleasant or distasteful.
I am firmly convinced that the problem of mental illness, its causes, treatment and care contains all the ingredients which demand a sense of urgency on the part of parliament and the public. I hope that after our discussion many others will share my view.
Sickness of the mind and in some instances of the nervous system is one of the most critical areas of our pattern of national health, and yet all too many of us choose to ignore its very existence because society-as society has so often done in the past in respect to disease-has placed a stigma upon it. Not so many years ago, cancer was spoken of in hushed tones and the families and friends of those afflicted with this dreadful ailment were ashamed to admit to anyone that someone close to them was suffering from it. The same is true today of mental sickness.
During the past 15 years we have uttered brave and enlightened words, saying that the mentally ill are sick people and should be treated in just the same way as other sick people. Some may say we have made progress, but their statements will not be borne out by the facts. It is true, Mr. Speaker, that we now call it mental "health" rather than mental "illness" or sickness. It is true that we no longer say a person who is sick of mind is insane. It is true that we

no longer term institutions which treat and care for the mentally ill as asylums, but call them hospitals. It is also true that public opinion permits general hospitals to house psychiatric wards. But such progress is pitifully small when compared with the magnitude of the problem.
I am afraid, Mr. Speaker, that our deeds have not matched our words, either in our attitudes or in our recognition of the needs of the mentally ill in a modern society in terms of treatment and care. Unfortunately we lag behind other countries, some smaller and less affluent than Canada, both in our attitude and in our resolve to deal realistically with the problem.
One of Canada's leading authorities on mental illnesses, Dr. C. A. Roberts, director of the Verdun Protestant hospital in Montreal and a former member of the staff of the Department of National Health and Welfare, had some very direct comments to make about the attitude of Canadians toward mental health. It seems to me that he put the case very well when he wrote in the September 17, 1960 issue of the Canadian Medical Association's journal:
For many years, lip service has been given to the principle that the mentally ill are sick people and should be treated as such. In spite of this, there is little indication of any widespread or real acceptance of this statement. There is hardly a measure available which does not confirm the terrific differences which exist in the attitudes of the community and of public authorities toward mental illness as compared with existing attitudes to physical illness.
Dr. Roberts then suggests that the professional workers in the mental health field perhaps have failed to state their case clearly and bring it to the attention of the public generally. In further comments on the failures of the public he wrote:
It is also possible that the public authorities and the community have such guilt about their attitudes toward the mentally ill and the inadequate treatment services which they provide that they are like the ostrich which hides its head in the sand.
They know that the problem exists but by denying it they no longer see it.
I sometimes feel that they hope to wake up some morning and find it gone.
If they feel this way, they will be disappointed, as the problem will be with us until adequate services for all types are provided to deal with it.
I think, Mr. Speaker, this is one of those painful truths which suggest-I would even go so far as to say demand-that parliament must take the initiative by insisting that something should be done through government departments and resources. If we fail to act, it will be a sorry commentary upon us and upon the society in which we live.
Many of us often wonder what mental illness really is. Some call it a nervous breakdown, others instability; still others suggest

that a mentally ill person is high strung and not a few, cling to the past, call it insanity. It is a disease which bewilders almost everyone. When we are told that someone close to us is mentally ill all sorts of fears come to our mind. Our thinking and our reactions are frequently fanned by a sense of shame. We are gripped by a sense of hopelessness. Our imagination races onward by the stories we have read, by plays we have seen or movies we have watched. The authors of these vehicles of entertainment may have used, legitimately, the licence of exaggeration to weave a story which would grasp the attention of their audiences. And this is fair; the audience wants to be entertained and not necessarily informed. Humour, which is so often cruel, has distorted our attitude toward the mentally ill and toward the retarded. Psychiatrists have been kidded, the couch has become a common butt of jokes, and even some of the earliest professional personalities associated with mental health, such as Freud, have not escaped the lash of cruel wit.
I think too that our concept of and our attitude toward mental sickness are based upon the tales we heard at our parents' knees. In other words, Mr. Speaker, we seldom think of mental health in modern terms, and know little of the tremendous advances which have been made by the psychiatric branch of medicine in the treatment, care and cure of mental illness.
If I might attempt a short definition, I would say that mental illness is a disability of thinking, of feeling and of behaviour. As a disease it has a variety of illnesses varying in severity, just as physical illness has. In other words, it can be as mild as a common cold or as severe and crippling as some cancers. Diagnostic techniques and the accumulated knowledge of psychiatry acquired through research, observation and experience permit the recognition and ultimate treatment of the specific type of mental illness, just as similar knowledge and techniques permit the accurate diagnosis of a physical illness.
Mental illnesses range in scope from anxiety alcoholism, drug addiction and geriatrics or senility to the more severe forms of paranoia and schizophrenia. Retardation also comes within the field of mental health. As a disease it requires preventive as well as curative facilities. Early diagnosis, treatment and proper care are as vital to the mentally ill as they are to the physically ill, even more so if those who are afflicted are to be restored to sound mental health and again become useful members of the community. Rehabilitation of the ability to earn a living and perform normal daily duties is now a prospect which the mentally ill, dependent 90205-6-32J
Mental Illness Survey
upon the severity of their illness, can look forward to just as do those who suffer serious damage to their limbs and who not so many years ago would have been maimed for life.
But the doctors in the field of mental health are the first to admit that, although great strides have been made in psychiatric treatment, the lack of facilities and funds for research are preventing this field of medicine from coming abreast with the field of physical medicine. The prospects are heartening, but our society cannot yet benefit from the full potential.
I think this may interest the house slightly. Statistics published by the dominion bureau of statistics-the latest available are for 1958-tell a startling story. In 1958, 47 per cent of all patients resident in hospitals in Canada were in psychiatric hospitals or psychiatric units of other hospitals. Tuberculosis institutions housed 8 per cent of all patients, while other types of sickness accounted for 45 per cent. Psychiatric hospitals and units and training schools for mental deficients housed approximately 75,000 Canadians. Each year 40,000 patients are admitted to these institutions and an equal number are discharged.
Current estimates place the number of alcoholics in Canada at more than 200,000. Three thousand Canadians are classified as drug addicts. I imagine few Canadians realize that 1,800 of their fellow citizens commit suicide each year.
These figures only tell part of the story. In a speech last March in Stratford, Ontario the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Monteith) said, and my source is the monthly publication of the mental health division of his department:
Other authorities have thrown the net even wider and maintain that a large proportion ot the people seen by their family doctor suiter from some degree of emotional disability.
If you refer to supplement No. 37 to Canada's Health and Welfare, published by the information division of the Department of National Health and Welfare and dealing with the world mental health year, you find this:
At least two thirds of the patients who visit their family doctor, it is estimated, suffer some degree of psychiatric disability.
The minister had referred earlier in his Stratford speech, if I may call it that, which was delivered on March 26, 1960 in the city of Stratford, to the fact that approximately 75,000 Canadians were housed in psychiatric accommodation. In the same speech the minister referred to a recent study carried out in Ontario which suggests-and I now quote the minister-

Mental Illness Survey
One out of every fifteen Canadians will spend some part of his life in mental hospitals of one kind or another.
These statistics, Mr. Speaker, may tell a startling story, but they are no more startling than the prospects contained in the Ontario study. Indeed, I think the two coupled together add validity to the statement, and again I quote from the summary of the minister's Stratford speech:
Health authorities in Canada ... considering all the evidence-precise and otherwise-have come to the conclusion that mental illness is the "largest special medical and hospital problem in Canada today, if not the greatest public health challenge of our time."
The financial burden for the treatment and care of the mentally ill falls on the provincial governments. While the psychiatric wards of general hospitals qualify a patient for benefits available under the hospital insurance and diagnostic services program, those hospitalized in mental hospitals do not receive such benefits. This places an unfair load on the relatives of such patients and upon the provinces. It does not assure the best in care or accommodation. If I had the time I would certainly expand on that last statement.
Some studies have shown that less is spent on the housing of the mentally ill than is spent on the housing of inmates in our penitentiaries. In the April 2, 1960 issue of the Canadian Medical Association Journal, page 733, a table of figures is published which sets out the cost per day per patient. Thus it is shown that in a general hospital the cost per patient per day is $15.11; in a tuberculosis sanatorium the cost is $8.50 per patient per day; in a chronic and convalescent hospital the cost is $5.77 per patient per day; in a federal penitentiary the cost per day of a prisoner is $5.66, while in a mental hospital the cost per day of a patient is $3.69.
The federal government will spend eight and three quarter million dollars on mental care through the annual mental health grants. These grants, as hon. members know, were instituted in 1948 and have been approved by parliament, in varying amounts, each year since that date. According to the minutes of the treasury board for March 3, 1960 the money is distributed on the basis of $25,000 to each province, with the balance being paid out to the provinces on the basis of a per capita allotment. The minister has stated:
For 1960-61, It is expected that an additional $750,000 in mental health grant funds will be used to carry forward research.
While the minister may argue, as he did in his Stratford speech, that in the past 12 years the government, through the mental health grants, has spent $54,500,000 on mental health, those concerned with mental health and the care and treatment of the mentally ill do

not consider the money being made available adequate to cope with the situation. The minister has said that the federal government has spent $4,500,000 on research alone in a 10-year period; that is, at a rate of less than half a million dollars a year. The amount allotted to research this year, according to the minister, will be required to support 60 projects.
If the problem of mental health is of the magnitude suggested by the minister in his Stratford speech, I should think he would urge a more generous policy in respect to research and mental health than the present government has approved. Certainly, if it is "the public health challenge of our time", far more money will be required.
The amount of $54,500,000 also appears very small when you consider what the money has been asked to do. For example, it has been asked to support certain services in mental hospitals, to assist in the development of new approaches in the treatment of mental illness in general hospitals through a form of out-patient clinics, to assist the training of personnel, and to support research.
I feel quite sure that the minister will ask me what my party did when we were in office, and he will undoubtedly tell the house that his government has been more generous than its predecessor. Before he makes that challenge I would like to tell him this. It was a Liberal government which initiated the mental health grants, together with all the other forms of medical and hospital assistance. The grants were increased at about the same rate by the Liberal government as they are currently being increased by the present government.
He should also bear in mind that for a good number of years, during the 12-year period 1948-1960, the Liberal government was initiating a program of health assistance undreamed of by any previous government. This program not only included the health grants but also the program of making bed grants for hospital construction in which psychiatric hospitals were included.
I think the house, Mr. Speaker, would be interested in hearing what other countries are doing in the field of mental health. In the United States a joint commission, supported by a grant from the congress of $1,250,000, has recently completed its work. The commission's job was to conduct a survey of mental health and mental illness in that country. The commission, formed in 1956, recorded its work and recommendations in the form of six to eight monographs, of which three have already appeared.

In the United Kingdom a royal commission report-this is rather interesting; the commission was established in 1954 and submitted its report in 1957-resulted in the passage of a mental health act by parliament in August, 1959. The terms of reference of the commission were to study laws relating to mental illness and mental deficiency. The minister of health of the United Kingdom- at that time Mr. Derek Waiter-Smith-said on second reading of the bill that its two main principles were:
(a)	that as much treatment as possible, both in the hospital and outside, should be given on a voluntary and informal basis, and
(b)	that proper provision should be made for the residual category of cases where compulsion is necessary, either in the interest of the patient or of society.
The contents of the bill, of which there is an excellent review in the June, 1960 issue of Canada's Mental Health, a publication of the Department of Health and Welfare, are not important to this discussion. But what I think is significant and important is the action taken by the government of the United Kingdom. In establishing the royal commission the government acknowledged that the then existing law was out of date; that it was not in tune with the times, nor with the attitude of the British public. The government of the United Kingdom recognized the need for a survey and assessment of the current situation so that it could act wisely. It complemented the work in the field of mental health which had already been done under the national health program.
Here in Canada the last time a survey was undertaken similar to that conducted by the United States joint commission or by the royal commission in Britain was in the period 194950. The survey was carried out by the provinces at the expense of the federal treasury. I think the survey was started about the time the government of the day announced the provision of mental health grants.
The results of the survey were published in 1951. Since that time there has been an enormous development in scientific knowledge concerning the nature and treatment of mental illness. New trends have emerged in the organization of treatment services, which may well place our present system of mental hospital services hopelessly and completely out of date.
At the present time Dr. J. S. Tyhurst professor of psychiatry at the University of British Columbia, is chairman of a standing committee on mental health services of the Canadian Mental Health Association. The committee was created before congress set up the joint commission in the United States. But the Tyhurst committee, which is studying many of the problems examined by the
Mental Illness Survey
joint commission, has had tar tougher sailing than its counterpart south of the border. Its existence has been threatened several times because of the lack of funds. Efforts to secure financial support from public and private sources in Canada were not fruitful, but the work of the committee has been of such significance that two large United States foundations have made grants so it could carry on its work.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that these financial difficulties suggest, as do the attitudes of the British and United States governments, that such a survey must be undertaken by the	central government and
supported by it financially. The time has come, Mr. Speaker, when Canada, on the initiative of the federal government, must take an inventory of the mental health program, of the state of its mental services, and examine all matters and legislation related to mental health and illness with a view to charting our course for the next ten years. The scope of the inquiry should include the group of areas mentioned by Dr. Roberts in the September 24, 1960 issue of the Canadian Medical Association's journal.
I am going to impose on hon. members and read this, because it is very basic to the argument. At page 708 of the Canadian Medical Association's journal of September 24, 1960 Dr. Roberts says:
The development of community mental health services is dependent on a number of factors, amongst the most important of which are:
1.	A clear understanding by the community of the needs of psychiatric patients.
2.	A complete redrafting of all legislation dealing with mental illness. These revisions should cover the Criminal Code, immigration and sick mariners legislation, the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act, the Penitentiaries Act, the mental hospital and related acts in all of the provinces, and the various curatorship or protection acts.
3.	The development of comprehensive services ranging from consultation and out-patient departments through day and night care to in-patient services based on the in-patient beds of community mental hospitals strategically located throughout the country.
4.	Separate facilities for psychopaths, criminals, addicts, the mentally retarded and other special psychosocial conditions.
5.	The provision of supporting rehabilitation programs-halfway houses, sheltered workshops, vocational training centres, foster homes, welfare institutions and so on.
6.	A meaningful involvement of the community through citizen participation on boards of hospitals, clinics and other services, and extensive expansion of volunteer programs.
7.	More adequate research-not only into specific conditions but to assess clinical services and develop new methods of treatment and organization.
I maintain that the inquiry should also include an assessment of the various research projects in mental health now being carried on in Canada. The purpose of this phase of the inquiry would be to advise the government

Mental Illness Survey
on the adoption of a program of research which would eliminate waste and duplication and also assure the country that its intellectual and financial resources are engaged to the best advantage. The inquiry should be a co-operative effort enlisting the support and assistance-indeed, the active participation-of the provinces and the other groups I have mentioned in my resolution.
The situation is urgent. This precludes the government from agreeing in principle to the value and importance of such a survey, yet saying that it cannot afford to spend the money. The sum required is not great. But, more important, the country cannot stand the spectacle of one government department saying this is "perhaps the greatest challenge of our time in the field of public health" and another saying "this is very true, but you cannot have the money".
This is something the two ministers must resolve between themselves. The money should be made available either through an increase in the department's budget or through a reduction of some other expropriation within the department. The Minister of Health and Welfare and the Minister of Finance need no reminder from me, I feel sure, that such a survey could result in savings to the government in future years through the more efficient use of the money available for mental health, and through the adoption of new measures and techniques to deal with this illness. I think, too, that the people of Canada, as well as the Minister of Finance, would be interested in learning what mental health and the treatment and care of the mentally ill will cost Canada in the predictable future. It would also help in the drafting of a long range program of facilities for the mentally ill, and for research.
In closing I want to stress two basic points. The first is the need for initiative on the part of the government in the area of mental health. The second is the great urgency of the challenge of mental illness. Canada has played an important role in contributing to solution of world problems over the past decade. The field of mental health is another area in which Canada could make a major contribution if the government would seize the initiative and undertake a national study to assess the whole problem of mental health in terms of the community's responsibility.
Next summer the world federation for mental health will hold an international conference in Paris at which representatives of 50 countries, including Canada, will be present. In 1961, psychiatrists from all over the world will gather in Montreal to attend the biennial conference of the international organization. The year 1960 is mental health year. For all these reasons the time is very appropriate for

Canadian initiative in a large scale survey of the problem. The Canadians who attend these conferences would be far better equipped to contribute to the discussions if they had such a study undertaken in their own country.
The last point I wish to stress is the sense of urgency which should pervade our thinking on the subject of mental health. A glance at the statistics bears out this urgency. Can we afford to wait when one of every 12 to 16 Canadians born today will be treated in a mental hospital; when three to four persons in every 1,000 of our population are confined to our mental hospitals, and when in spite of all the new and improved services, admissions to mental hospitals are increasing by 20 to 25 per cent each year? I ask, can we afford to wait? It has been said in truth that a nation's health is a nation's wealth. Well, our wealth is imperilled.
I commend this resolution to all hon. members.

subtopic: SUGGESTED NATIONAL SURVEY OF EXTENT OF MENTAL ILLNESS
speechtext:
On rising to take part in this debate I wish to congratulate the hon. member who has just spoken for a most comprehensive survey of a very difficult situation and for the way in which he has presented certain facts, as well as for the emotional appeal he made to the house to consider certain steps which he believes should be taken. I mean these words of congratulation to be very warm and sincere.
I do not think anyone in this house would deny that we are dealing with a very serious and important problem when we speak of mental health in Canada, or that there are things which need to be done. The hon. member has mentioned a number of them. He mentioned, in particular, the question of the terminology applied to patients, and certain activities which need to be undertaken as extensions of existing procedures, with regard to which there is no disagreement and, indeed, no problem.
I think in most cases progress is now being made along these lines. I was very pleased to hear the hon. member note that there has been a considerable improvement in facilities in recent years. That, of course, is coupled with an improvement in the understanding shown by the general public in connection with mental illness. The hon. member mentioned the change in name to mental illness, a name which has replaced previous terms which were in themselves of the type to frighten these unfortunate people and tend to isolate them from the rest of society, words such as "insane" and "demented".
I should like to emphasize one point he made with regard to the institutional care of the mentally ill, because in an earlier period these people were committed or sentenced by a court to enter certain of these institutions,

and in at least some cases they were housed in buildings which had been discarded as jails because they were unfit for habitation even by the type of person accommodated in jails in that period. Thus over the years there has been progress.
The hon. member also mentioned that perhaps the terminology used nowadays is more acceptable than once it was, but that a further improvement is desirable. This is an educational matter. Back in 1905 or 1910 one could only use the word "consumption" or the word "tuberculosis" in a hushed voice. The newspaper accounts of that day spoke of people "going into a decline". The word "tuberculosis" was a frightening and dirty word. Today, however, the public accepts the term, as it has slowly come to accept the term "venereal disease" as being diseases of a communicable nature which, whatever else one may think about them, are diseases which have to be treated as communicable diseases.
I would suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that as much if not more progress has been made in the public's attitude toward mental illness. In fact, at the present time there may be some danger of an obsession in the public mind as a result of which mental illness or mental health is more to the foreground than is desirable in relation to other aspects of the health program in our community, thus causing an imbalance. I rather think if we could lift our sights in connection with other aspects of our health problems to the level from which we are now looking at mental health, the whole general situation and the health of the people of Canada would be infinitely improved.
The hon. member also spoke in favour of federal money being granted to assist provincial governments in undertaking a national study in connection with a number of projects which he mentioned. I do not decry this, but I would like to point out that before the 1948 health grants came into being a large number of provincial governments, in particular the one with which I am most familiar, that of the province of Ontario, had made a study of existing facilities, the training of personnel and the planning which needed to be developed in order to meet the demands of this known problem in the community, a problem of increasing proportions because of the social disturbances consequent on the second world war.
I do not think any government or group of people should take unto themselves the role of the only ones to do anything about this question, and I am sure the hon. member was not advocating that this should be the case. But I should like to pay my tribute to those who have associated themselves, in the name of the Canadian Mental Health
Mental Illness Survey
Association, with the publicizing of this question for the very good briefs they have presented to the government with the object of increasing the interest of the general population and providing ways and means toward a more effective solution of this whole problem.
I wish to direct my attention specifically to the language of the resolution. The hon. member has stated the need for a national survey of the extent of mental illness, its causes, problems and methods of treatment. I submit that in the presentation of his case the hon. member did not fully develop the language he has used in the resolution. While I sincerely agree with the object of his approach, I do feel the resolution itself needs to be examined for what it is.
When you consider the matter of mental illness you are using here a collective term which includes a number of mental disorders and disabilities of one kind and another. Therefore the various component parts of this inclusive term must not only be clearly set forth and understood but clearly acceptable to those Who are making such a survey. While in the main much of this could be done at the present time, there still would be a large area in which common agreement would be difficult to achieve.
I say this because we are now including in mental illness not only such problems as mental retardation-that is deficiency of mental capacity-but also disorders such as epilepsy, the mental stages which occur in senility, especially those arising from arteriosclerosis, the severe functional psychotic conditions of various kinds, the psychoneuroses and a group that are simply classed as disorders of character and behaviour.
If we are going to deal with a survey of existing legislation, methods and arrangements, that is not an extensive matter, and I suggest that it is in large part already under way or already recommended and such study as can be made has been made. But if you are going to make a survey to determine the extent of mental illness you will be attempting to determine the quantity of mental illness, and that amount or quantity is influenced by what is included under the heading.
Therefore in dealing with mental illness you are dealing with a state of departure from mental health. Health is a relative term. Health is not the absence of disorders but a positive state, and that positive state does exist in degree. Mental illness is a departure from it, and therefore can be measured only in degree by that departure. This in itself constitutes a difficulty which may be insurmountable in conducting a true survey of

Mental Illness Survey
this type because of the problem of determining the degree of departure from health to illness.
This, of course, to a large extent would be concerned with the various forms of psychoneuroses in which are included anxiety reactions, hysterical reactions, obsessive compulsive reactions, neurotic depressive reactions, somatization reactions and others as well as a number of things which are set forth collectively because they are lacking in numbers to designate them as a separate classification if such classification could be produced.
It is in this area that I would have hoped the hon. member would have specified more clearly what he meant by the extent of mental illness in recommending that a survey take place, because the type of survey recommended, one must assume from the language employed, would not only be difficult to carry out but would require the services of a large number of highly trained and skilled people who are already engaged in various clinical specialities of psychology and psychiatry.
It would also be a very expensive undertaking. Not only would this mean that persons who are now having an extremely difficult time coping with the load of known disabilities which come and are coming under treatment and benefit would be put on a survey which in my opinion would be of questionable value but it would also add to an already difficult situation. Nor should the question of cost be forgotten. The cost would be determined by how much you wanted to do. A full survey as described in the language of the resolution would be extremely expensive. One would also have to weigh the advantage of taking personnel away from the important work which they are already doing and which perhaps they should be left to do.
I think this is borne out as an opinion by what we now know about mental illness. We have available some excellent publications on the subject. One of these to which I should like to make reference is the mental health statistics of the dominion bureau of statistics. I hold in my hand the volume for 1958. The table of contents, which is very inclusive, indicates that it deals with such questions as an historical summary, first admissions, the problem of readmissions, the question of discharges, deaths, transfers and institutional information.
To augment some of the words which my hon. friend has already used I think one should point out that at page 12 of this volume a table is set forth showing the capacity and patient load by province of the type of mental institutions in Canada. Because I do not believe it is generally known I feel I should point out to the house that there is a

bed capacity of 42,743 in public mental hospitals. In addition, there is a bed capacity of 1,375 in mental hospitals coming directly under the federal government.

subtopic: SUGGESTED NATIONAL SURVEY OF EXTENT OF MENTAL ILLNESS
speechtext: What was the first total?

subtopic: SUGGESTED NATIONAL SURVEY OF EXTENT OF MENTAL ILLNESS
speechtext:
Public mental hospitals, 42,743; federal hospitals, 1,375; county and municipal mental hospitals, 2,089; private, 80, and so on. There is a long list of these. I simply use this as an illustration to show that we already know about a variety of things in this field and it would not be necessary to engage further in an excess of research for certain material.
Also dealt with in this publication is the question of diagnostic distinction by agreed nomenclature. The nomenclature in this instance follows the international list of the diseases, injuries and causes of death which are the basis for our vital statistics.
I think the following is particularly important. The publication also gives a breakdown of diagnosis by age, sex and provincial area. In this volume we have a large amount of valuable information. I shall return to that subject In a few minutes, if I may.
Where you are dealing with problems that can be and are as common to one area of the country as to the other, by diagnosis, affliction, age and sex, the basic element in each of these problems is exactly the same. The numbers may bother us, but inquiring into the cause and effect can be done just as well in one part of the country as in another. It may be done as well by a few people as by many. Therefore, because we know the vast numbers of those people across Canada who suffer from the same thing, it does not necessarily mean that volume is going to help us now to discover the cause, the treatment and the hoped-for cure and possibly the prevention of any particular disability.
I should also like to say that such a survey as the hon. member mentions could be pretty expensive. It depends on the extent. I mentioned before that a limited review could be done without a great deal of cost. Perhaps it is being undertaken.
I should like to refer to the amount ol money which is being spent in Canada at the present time, and I go back to the figures quoted as to the national health grants instituted by the former government in 1948. In those figures we see a rather interesting fact, namely that the provision originally made for mental health in 1948-49 was some $4 million. Of that amount only $439,128 could be used in that year. This I think is a story which shows the small number of personnel available at that time and the lack of appropriate procedures to deal with some of the

problems that needed investigation. For 195960 the amount available is $7,234,868, of which there has been an over-utilization, because the spending is listed as $7,690,719. In the 12 years the total amount available for all the provinces was $74 million plus. The amount spent was $57 million plus, or roughly 77 per cent of the amount available. The reason it was not 100 per cent, I submit, was the absence of sufficient personnel and procedures to deal with the known problems.
I should like to compare that with what has been spent by the federal government in general public health grants for the same period of time. These grants are in a sense made to augment, supplement and encourage health services in the provinces in one way or another. This grant is not inseparable from all other grants but rather is complementary to all other grants in a variety of ways. In this 12-year period the spending has been again $57 million plus, perhaps not $200,000 more than the total amount of federal spending on mental health grants in the same period of time.
My hon. friend quoted from a publication called Canada and World Mental Health Year, which is put out by the world health association in collaboration with the Canadian Mental Health Association. I should like to direct the hon. member's attention to additional information which he did not find necessary to use in his own remarks. In this period of 12 years, of the $57 million spent only 52 per cent has gone to mental institutions, 12 per cent to mental health clinics, 11 per cent to psychiatric services in general hospitals, 8 per cent to research, 8 per cent to bursaries, 6 per cent to training programs, and 3 per cent to provincial mental health divisions. This, sir, does not in any way represent the total spent because in addition-I give this as a small indication-you have provincial institutions, provincial programs which in themselves carry very substantial expenditures of money and are in addition to the amounts which are listed here as coming from the federal government.
Again I say, sir, that this matter of money as between the provinces and the dominion is not a matter of grants alone; it is a matter of the arrangements that are made for the federal and provincial governments to carry on their work. This we hope is something which will come a little closer to being a better method than we have had in the past. I very firmly believe that knowledge of problems is widely spread across Canada, and that people know of the problems in their own area perhaps better than those at a distance. In this particular instance the work of the Canadian Mental Health Association, with all its branches stimulating work in
Mental Illness Survey
communities and provinces, helps bring about a widespread understanding by local communities of problems and the need of caring for them.
I suggest to you, sir, that just as in Ontario in 1943, 1944 and 1945 and so on the techniques of much of the work now being done on mental health were begun, which came from a local understanding by the people of the need so they were prepared to spend money which came from them by way of taxes and do somehing for their own particular area, so today we must view the problem in the same light. I would not want to think that we can oversimplify too much this type of work, which will happen if we lose not only the community understanding but also the community responsibility.
Again I pay tribute to such organizations as the Canadian Mental Health Association for arousing interest. There are certain things which I should like to point out. The Canadian Mental Health Association has submitted briefs to the government from time to time. They just submitted one, as a matter of fact, on December 2, three days ago, to the Prime Minister and the cabinet. On page 7 they had this to say about mental health grants:
These grants were established by the federal government in 1945 in order to provide encouragement to the provincial governments in their efforts to establish adequate preventive, diagnostic, treatment and rehabilitation services and research in the field of mental illness and health. The original policy was to provide a small uniform grant to all provinces and then to make the balance of the money up to $4 million available on a per capita basis. The grant to any one province was not to exceed one fifth of the total moneys expended by the provincial and local governments on mental health programs during the fiscal year. Although the provinces were a little slow at first in making use of these grants, they are now eagerly utilizing them fully. The amount of money available in these grants was increased yearly until a maximum was reached in the middle 1950's. This ceiling remained in spite of a rapidly increasing population and a swift development of psychiatric facilities, until the present government again raised the amount available (1960) to more than $8 million.
When one considers spending the cost of the proposed survey, one has to judge whether that amount of the money which is now being spent on mental health and and the needs in the mental health field should be used for such a survey, because among those areas of need are the increased number of units for psychiatric care. There is need for a further and more intensive study of the suitability of care methods. Psychiatric units in general hospitals is not exactly a new idea.
In a publication by Dr. Gilbert, who was former chief of the mental health division of the Department of National Health and Welfare, some aspects of the mental health situation in Canada during 1958 are given, and

Mental Illness Survey
they are reprinted by the kind permission of the author and publisher in the Medical Services Journal of January, 1960. He has a paragraph here from which I should like to quote a few words. It reads as follows:
The psychiatric unit in a general hospital is by no means a new venture . .. the first units on this continent were conceived about one hundred years ago in connection with the New York hospital and the Pennsylvania hospital. These were really clearing houses, similar to those established later at Albany and Toronto, and for some time these units remained places where those who could make a quick recovery . .. were separated from those who needed long term care in a mental hospital.
I use this to show that there is no single facility that one can have to deal with mental illness but rather it is a matter of a variety of facilities. There is need for certain types of mental hospitals that are not merely hospitals for the custodial care of the residual mental population because we lack some means of sheltering them, as so unfortunately was the case in the past. Methods of treatment now, as is the case with many other illness, have developed to a great extent. The hope of alleviation or possible cure is considerably greater than it ever has been before; therefore the thing to do at the moment is to have such facilities as are possible at the community level for the recognition of these earliest stages of depart-ture from mental health into mental illness and for their prompt treatment.
This is necessary for the reduction of mental illness in this country, because in large part the bulk of mental illness is capable of remedy. Unfortunately we do have large numbers of mentally retarded. Unfortunately we do have numbers who are epileptics but who have now been brought under control and have been able to take their places in society. We do have a very substantial number of the functional psychotic cases, but we have an unconscionable amount of psychoneuroses of great variety in manner and form which is perhaps attributable to the stresses and strains of our way of life.
This is not just a hospital unit problem, not a mental hospital problem, but a problem of the society in which we live. Therefore we need research of two kinds. First we need research into the actual illness itself, research that is physiological and biochemical in its character. This type of research into particular illnesses does not have to be done in bulk; it can be done among small units of the same type.
There is another type of investigation which is on a wider basis and which we call epidemiological investigation. If hon. members will forgive me, the word "epidemiology" is not known to everybody. It is a word which

literally means "upon the people". It suggests there is some overwhelming thing which has come down upon the people and therefore it is essentially used in medicine for those conditions which exist in large numbers or mass or volume in a community. It was first used as far back as ancient days, and had particular reference then to communicable diseases such as plague and pox of one kind or another. Now, with the communicable disease situation improved, much the same type of technique is being used to investigate non-communicable disabilities, and it is common terminology that is used with respect to the investigation of such conditions from an epidemiological standpoint.
Just as research of a physiological or biochemical nature may be undertaken in a single instance, so research in a community may have a tremendous bearing upon what else goes on in other communities. It is not necessary to do research in all communities. One can do it on a sample basis if the sample has been properly selected. There is one quotation I should like to refer to here and it comes again from the same publication by J. E. Gilbert. Under the heading "Research" there is the following:
Of interest to all those working in the field of mental health will be the publication, later on this year, of the results from one of the largest epidemiological investigations in the field of mental disorder. This inquiry has taken place, during the past ten years, in the province of Nova Scotia and has been supported by the province together with assistance from federal health grants and from other institutions in the United States. Preliminary reports indicate that this research will show, perhaps for the first time, the true nature and extent of mental illness in a community.
As my time is drawing short, Mr. Speaker, I should like to come back closer to the terms of the resolution. Here the hon. member is asking for a survey not only of the extent of mental illness but also of the causes, the problems that exist and methods of treatment.
The causes of mental illness are the function of research. I have described the two main types of research which can exist. From intensive studies of both these kinds and related work, progress can be made by concentrating personnel and funds upon problems which are common to the whole. The completeness of such studies is more important than spreading workers and money thinly over a wider area. The causes, problems and methods of treatment would therefore seem to be best dealt with by present procedures to which more financial encouragement might be given.
Therefore, sir, I submit that in spite of the excellent presentation my hon. friend has made, most of his arguments were directed not to the wording of the resolution but to

a condition which we all know exists and about which steps are being taken in some measure. However, I find that the words of the resolution detract from it to this extent, that the matter of causes, problems and methods of treatment is under study. In my view these activities should have the first call upon available funds. With regard to the extent of mental illness, its quantity, in large part the load of the severely mentally ill, is known and much of what might with difficulty be determined by a survey is not of such an urgent nature as to demand the withdrawal of personnel from their present work, which could be detrimental to their carrying out their present occupations.
Therefore I submit the resolution has real merit in pointing up the problem and the program. I believe that the government has already taken some steps to meet the more pressing problems, and no doubt we will hear from the minister in this connection. It is hoped that this effort will not only continue but will be augmented as circumstances permit so that the things which the hon. member has mentioned will come about in actual fact.

subtopic: SUGGESTED NATIONAL SURVEY OF EXTENT OF MENTAL ILLNESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the introduction of this most commendable resolution gives the house an opportunity to consider and discuss what is without doubt a most important and serious problem in Canada. Personally I am very pleased that the resolution is drafted so as to be all inclusive, in that there is recognition of the advisability of greater co-operation among all levels of government and professional and other groups with regard to mental illness. There is also a reference to the necessity of making a national survey of the extent of mental illness, its causes, problems and methods of treatment.
I am not going to deal in any way at all with the technicalities of the terminology of the resolution. I intend to deal only with the serious problem which had been drawn to our attention and with the intent and object of the resolution. If I may say so, sir, I was most disappointed, though not surprised, at some of the remarks just made by the hon. member for Durham (M. Vivian). He commented, in the latter part of his remarks, upon the wording of the resolution. That is not important in this debate. This resolution, it should be recognized, was introduced as a vehicle to carry the discussion of this important matter.
May I also say, and this is all I am going to remark about the hon. member, that he also disappointed though he did not surprise me with the emphasis he placed on the cost. He repeated more than once the fact that there would be a tremendous expenditure
Mental Illness Survey
connected with this matter if a real survey were made and if real action were taken to tackle this vital problem.
Undoubtedly it would be expensive; undoubtedly it would cost a great deal of money. However, Mr. Speaker, I have no hesitation in saying that from the point of view of the amount of money that might be involved it is going to cost a lot more if you do not invest money now to tackle the problem. The social cost alone will be heavy, but the cost of hospitalization and treatment, perhaps care for life, will be heavier. I say, sir, that any money spent now is a good investment and will save a lot more money in the future.
I am not going to discuss this matter from the point of view of the statistics for the whole of Canada, because that has been done by the mover of this resolution. However, in order to emphasize the seriousness, the complexity of the problem I do want to say something about the province of British Columbia. I should like to mention also the new approach, the new thinking in connection with this problem, and how that can have most beneficial results.
In 1949 the number of admissions to all the mental institutions in British Columbia totalled 1,260. Ten years later, in 1959, the number of admissions to all British Columbia mental institutions was 2,993. This means that at the close of last year, in British Columbia mental institutions there were 9,975 persons. Perhaps the hon. member for Durham would be interested in the cost connected with this number of cases. Last year the maintenance expenditures by the province of British Columbia on its institutions totalled $12,453,445. The per capita cost of keeping a person in an institution for a year amounted to $1,993.38, and the daily cost was $5.46. When we face an increase in the numbers in our mental institutions, when we recognize the cost which I have just given, then I have no hesitation in saying that money spent now to avoid that type of expenditure in the future is good for the taxpayer, is good for the government and good for society in Canada.
Speaking of this great problem of mental illness, I think there is one phase of it which is of the utmost importance and to which no reference was made by the hon. member for Durham. I refer to the problem of the youth. In the 10-year period that I mentioned in British Columbia, 1,155 of those admitted were under 15 years of age. This is serious enough, Mr. Speaker; but admissions for voluntary treatment in the mental health centres of British Columbia last year-this is not institutions-numbered 1,745. Of these, 776 were children.

Mental Illness Survey
Surely, sir, if we have any responsibilities at all-and we have many-one of the greatest is the care of those who are going to take our places. Money spent now on these children is a social investment. Money spent now on surveys, on understanding the problem, on remedies and cures, I say is going to save us, in all probability, the necessity of spending this $1,993.38 per year on each of these children in the future in order to keep them in an institution.
Let us consider now the new approaches, the new studies and the new methods. We have in our Pacific province an institution known as the Crease clinic. It has been in existence for only about eight years. Prior to the establishment of the Crease clinic if you were mentally ill-of course then they did not call you mentally ill, they called you a lunatic-there was only one way to get treatment. You had to be declared a lunatic and committed to a mental institution. This situation has now been changed. As a result of the establishment of the Crease clinic you can go there for a period of not longer than four months and, if cured, you can then be discharged. If after these four months you cannot be cured, only then are you committed to an institution for the insane.
I believe this is of the utmost importance. At the end of 1958 there were 252 in residence in the Crease clinic. In 1959 there were 1,992 new admissions, which means that for the year 1959 we had 1,744 in the Crease clinic who were mentally ill. But, sir, of those 1,744, during that 12-month period 1,411 were discharged into the community as cured. They were sent back into society to make their contribution to society, and were no longer an expense on the taxpayer.
There is also another interesting point. Previously, one had to be committed to an insane asylum. However, under this system if one knows one is mentally ill-and there is no stigma to being mentally ill-one can voluntarily enter the Crease clinic the same as one would go into a hospital for any other physical disability. I believe this is a most interesting and heartening thing. In 1959, in British Columbia, 56 per cent of these patients voluntarily committed themselves to the Crease clinic for treatment.
These are some of the things which are comparatively new in the treatment of mental illness in Canada. They demonstrate what can be done when attention is paid to these problems. I am convinced that greater care and greater study in this field will eventually give rise to far greater advances in the future than we have seen in the past.
Now I want to mention one other aspect as far as the province of British Columbia is concerned. I do so again because of this

question of expense. In the province of British Columbia we have what is known as the Woodlands shool, which is an institution for imbeciles and senile people. Last year at Woodlands school there were 1,403 residents. However, whilst we had 1,403 residents in that institution it was not handling the problem, because there were 510 people on the waiting list who were not receiving the specialized care and medical attention which they so desperately need. I am certain that the Minister of National Health and Welfare recognizes that a continuation of that situation not only makes the problem more difficult for the individual concerned but is going to make the expense more heavy for those who have to pay for the institutionalizing of these people.
Therefore I say, Mr. Speaker, that no matter how you look at the problem, it is a vast one, a vital one, a serious one. Although much has been accomplished or is being accomplished now, no matter what money is being spent now there is a great deal more to be done. We cannot let the matter rest, because the longer we leave it alone, or the longer we do not intensify our surveys, our studies, our analyses, the more we are going to be troubled with this problem and the greater will be the eventual expense.
I do not agree with anybody who says these things are impossible, that the object or the purpose in the mind of the mover of this resolution is impossible. There is only one definition of "impossible"; that is, that which has not yet been done. That comes very clearly to mind from my own experience, and I think I should take a few moments to tell the house why that comes very clearly to mind. Back in 1933 we found that no elected member ever bothered to visit the mental institutions of British Columbia. We spoke to the medical superintendent of that day, and he said he could not remember ever seeing an elected member with sufficient interest to visit the mental institutions.
There were some elected in 1933 who were interested. We were amazed to discover that once people were placed in a mental institution, they were forgotten. Some of them had been there for 15, 20, 25 years and had been forgotten. We were told they had been forgotten; nobody had any interest in them; nobody was prepared to sign them out, which the law required. There was no one to give them a home, find them a job or take them in during the transitional period from institutional to social life.
Therefore we raised the matter in the British Columbia legislature. We said, "Let us take people out of the insane asylums as well as put them in". I can well remember, although it is nearly 38 years ago, that we

were told we were crazy to think of taking people out of mental institutions as well as putting them in. I can remember as well as if it were yesterday that nearly all the criticism directed at us to the effect that we did not know what we were talking about came from medical men. The government would not do anything about it; it was impossible to take people out of these institutions. We ourselves, as individuals, raised the sum of $15,000 and bought a big home in Vancouver, and 20 or 25 years ago you could buy a big home for $15,000 in Vancouver. We hired a nurse trained in psychiatry and we hired two doctors who were interested in this work. We staffed and furnished this home. Then we went out to Essondale, the insane institution of British Columbia, and said to the medical superintendent-and I can remember the words as clearly now as though it were yesterday-"Have you any women in here who should not be in here?" He said, "Yes; how many do you want?"
So we started signing them out and putting them into this home which we had bought. After three months they were rehabilitated from the institution into society. They found a place to stay, a job to go to; they went, and somebody else was signed out of the institution. Over the years we operated that system not more than five, if my memory is correct, ever had to go back to an institution again.
Think of the saving of human life; think of the saving-if you want to think that way -of the taxpayers' dollar. That system was so successful in doing something that could not be done that after a few years the government bought the home and operates it to this very day. I know that out of that situation came the growing understanding of the need for this type of institution to which I have referred, the Crease clinic, and the new approach to mental health. This was a new approach, not only to get these people treated the same as people are treated for a broken arm or any other disease, but also as to the need for rehabilitation afterwards.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we in this group do not accept the word "impossible". We do not accept this "go slow" argument. We do not accept that it is going to cost too much money now. We think we who have the elected responsibility have to face up to the issue and the crisis. We have to think not only of the present but project our minds into the future as best we can on our analysis of this situation and see if we cannot do more than we are doing at the present time.
I do not decry for one moment all that provincial governments, the federal government and outside organizations have done and are doing. I most certainly agree, sir, with
Mental Illness Survey
the intent, the purport, the object of this resolution. We should ask the government to consider the advisability now of greater effort, with greater concentration in the field of surveys and studies on this most vital issue and on the entire question of mental illness, its causes, problems and methods of treatment.
I think the mover of this resolution should be most highly commended for having brought this matter so forcibly to our attention, for having given us such a broad outline. I hope it will receive the non-partisan consideration it deserves, and that as a result of our discussion this afternoon even greater progress will be made in the future than has been made in the past.

Mr. Speaker, I want to compliment the member for Mount Royal (Mr. Macnaughton) for introducing this resolution. It may be a little broader than it should be; however, the intent and purpose behind it I think are sincere, and I think it deserves as much consideration as we can give it.
The hon. member read some statistics for 1958 in connection with mental health, concerning the number of patients in institutions throughout the country. We admit that the number of first admissions has risen from 72 per 100,000 population to 156 per 100,000 population from 1932 to 1958, but on the other hand one has to remember that these are figures in connection with psychiatric institutions, and that our population has doubled.
We have a great number of inherent instabilities in this country. Members may or may not know about the famous family which immigrated to the United States when the United States was still a colony. In that group of immigrants were a moronic girl and boy. They later married and there are now, according to the latest reports, some 32,000 of their descendants in mental institutions, hopelessly incapable of facing our present civilization, in the United States of America.
These are alarming figures, but they do serve to explain the number of patients in institutions. Incidentally, I think the figures and statistics given create some interest because they show that the national male rate -that is, the number of male patients in institutions-is higher at every level of age than the female rate.
As has been noted, the cost is appalling, that is in straight money in order to maintain these institutions, provide the grants for mental health studies and help support other psychiatric institutions. But the cost is not only there; the cost is in human beings who are of no value to our country. There are other things besides, as has been mentioned

Mental Illness Survey
by the hon. member for Mount Royal; delinquency, alcoholism, drug addiction, absenteeism, job maladjustment-the old square peg in the round hole-and so on. The effect on industry of maladjusted people who have broken down under stress is fantastic. Unfortunately the psychiatrists are too uncertain about the structure and functions of industry to worry too much about the cost of absenteeism and its effect on the economy of the country.
Perhaps it would be as well to differentiate between mental health study and psychiatry. Psychiatry is the study of pathology, whereas mental health is a study of love communication and understanding beyond therapy and prevention into education and the social sciences. To date most of our research has been scientific, on pathological lines, and mainly concerned with the prevention and treatment of personality maladjustments, for instance the cause and manner of development of one of our greatest mental diseases, schizophrenia.
This, it seems, is coming closer to solution, but there have been two schools of thought in this whole process of evaluating mental health. There are those who feel that our rapid advance in urbanization and industrialization has resulted in conflict which in turn leads to neuroses. There are others who feel that our concern with mental health is merely an indication of our greater awareness of, and ability to diagnose, abnormalities of human behaviour, some of which are very slight. Psychiatry is a relatively new science and we may be too concerned about mild variations or mental aberrations with the result that too much importance is attached to them.
The only area of agreement between these two groups is that there is a greater need for research, not in any restricted area but on a national and international scale. In fact I think the former minister of health put it very well when he said that on the international scale it seemed strange that people forced into close proximity cannot live as neighbours. Our representatives on international bodies are called upon to interpret the feelings of their people without understanding them. Indeed, our tragedy is not international misunderstanding but an ignorance of where national aspirations must be pointed.
Perhaps we should not be too much concerned about stress and strain imposed by our present civilization on the minds of our people. Perhaps we are too prone to blame the fears of atomic war hanging over our heads, or international tension, for creating stresses which have really come down through the centuries. It is not these stresses

which are strange, I often feel; it is, rather, the inability of our people at the present time to cope with human relationships, or their jobs, or spiritual values.
Psychiatrists can sometimes diagnose certain of these stresses, but they seem unable to develop the ability to cope with them or to give any advice on how to treat them. Yet we cannot forget that it is in times of stress that are born some of the greatest ideas in the arts and sciences that man has ever conceived. Our great effort must be not to do away with the stresses-that come with civilization but to create in our people some ability to understand and live with these stresses. That great man Pasteur said over 50 years ago:
Two contrary laws seem to be wrestling with each other nowadays-the one a law of blood and death, ever forging new means of destruction and forcing nations to be constantly ready for the battlefield-
It seems strange that these words should be so applicable to this day, as they have been for many years past. To continue the quotation:
-the other a law of peace, work and health, ever evolving new means of delivering man from the scourges which mislead him. The one seeks violent conquest, the other the relief of humanity. The latter places one human life above any victory, while the former would sacrifice hundreds of thousands of lives to the ambition of one. Which of these laws shall ultimately prevail, God alone knows.
So Pasteur, in what we would now call those unlightened days, had a greater knowledge of what is facing us than we have, it seems. As the member for Mount Royal has stated, the United States has recognized this problem, and in a joint resolution which came before congress in 1955 it had this to say in part:
Whereas there seems to be a discouraging lag between the discovery of new knowledge and skills in treating mental illness and their widespread application, as is evidenced by the fact that only about one third of newly admitted mental patients are discharged from state hospitals in the course of a year, in a few outstanding institutions the recovery rate is 75 per centum or more-
Thus, although our institutions have advanced greatly over the past 25 years, there is still a marked lag in research not only in the prevention of these mental diseases but in their treatment and cure and in the restoration of the individuals concerned to the economic flow of the nation. Research into the field of mental diseases has lagged very far behind the rest of medical science. The prejudice, fear and mysticism of centuries seems to have been handed down to us unabated, and only a dedicated few have been left to give of their time, resulting in the amount of knowledge that we do possess concerning the dynamics of these mental aberrations.

I agree with those hon. members who have stated that research is far more important than treatment in this field. Through various government departments-I think particularly of the Department of Agriculture and the Department of National Defence-we have expended large sums of money on research. I believe the grant to the Department of Agriculture totals approximately $30 million, while the atomic research and related grants total approximately $41 million. Although we have doubled our research grants for mental health in the last year, bringing them to a total of $8 million, we are still lagging far behind in relation to the research grants given to other departments.
The difficulty involved' in giving a straight mental health grant is that these funds are not used solely for research but for mental health services as well. As a result there is less available for research. Simply increasing the grant for mental health will not result in too large an increase in that amount which should be set aside specifically for research into mental health.
The purpose of the resolution is clear and comprehensive. It is to widen the scope of the investigation in this field through increasing these grants. It may be true that the wording of the resolution should be more explicit in relating it to the field of research. However, any amount of money expended in this way will widen our knowledge of mental disorders and their causes.
I think it is more important to create the facilities which can guide, train and possibly even obviate these inner conflicts before they produce irreparable mental damage. I am sure all hon. members of the house will agree that this resolution is a very good one and should have the support of hon. members on every side of the chamber.

Mr. Speaker, my remarks will be very brief, because a good deal of what I had intended to say has already been covered by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch). I do wish, however, to commend the hon. member for Mount Royal for introducing this resolution at this time.
Mental illness is a national problem. If we are ever going to do anything worth-while about it we must recognize it as such and take steps to deal with it on a national scale. At the present time for the most part we are leaving it to the municipalities, to the provincial authorities and in some cases to private agencies. Almost without exception these do not have the resources to deal with the problem adequately.
Mental Illness Survey
Turning to the wording of the resolution, it asks the government to:
-consider the advisability of co-operating with the provincial authorities and such professional and other groups as may be interested, in making a national survey of the extent of mental illness, its causes, problems and methods of treatment.
In other words, it asks the federal government to take the initiative in organizing the very first step that must be taken if we are going to deal with the problem in a systematic manner. That first step is to make a survey so that we may have a clear idea of the extent and nature of the problem. Possibly we may also be able to discover some relationship between the incidence of mental illness and such things as poverty, tension and other conditions under which we live in this nuclear age.
Having made the survey I hope the government will be then encouraged to take the second step and work out a plan of action or a co-ordinated plan of attack. Some hon. members have referred to the cost involved in this undertaking, and no doubt the cost would be considerable; but if we mean business we should be able to work out a plan that would reduce the problem to proportions which can be dealt with in separate stages.
That is why I so strongly support the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver East. In my opinion the starting point in this survey and in the plan of action should be directed toward the young people. I will not deal with statistics because it is not necessary in a debate of this kind.
In travelling throughout our own districts and throughout the nation in general we have all personally encountered tragic cases of families who have been burdened with mentally retarded children whose affliction exists in varying degrees. Some families I know have had two such children. It is something with which they cannot deal themselves. I regret to say that in my own province no institution exists for that purpose. Some hon. members have told us of the good work that is being done in this field by certain private agencies. In my own province we have the Vera Perlin school which is a private organization under which schools are set up for mentally retarded youngsters. Here again, however, they can only scratch the surface of the problem. Most provinces are hard put to provide funds for the education of their normal children, and when it comes to subnormal children requiring specialized training, care and teaching they are unable to cope with the problem at all.
If we really believe that our human resources are our most valuable resources it seems to me we should put that belief into action by taking steps along the lines suggested in this resolution.

Mental Illness Survey

Mr. Speaker, I should first like to congratulate the hon. member for Mount Royal for introducing this resolution. In his introductory remarks the hon, member emphasized the need of an awareness on the part of the average Canadian of the problem of mental health. If this discussion today achieves nothing more than the focusing of the attention of the nation through its parliament on the subject of mental health, the hon. gentleman will have achieved a great deal in introducing the resolution.
It is interesting to note how the general attitude toward mental health has changed in the last few years. As the hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. Macnaughton) pointed out, there was a certain stigma attached to mental illness which has just about disappeared today. The attitude toward various forms of mental illness such as alcoholism and retardation in children has changed a great deal in the last few years. Everyone has a certain amount of sympathy for the alcoholic and attempts to assist him whenever possible. The attitude toward retarded children has completely changed. Formerly families were sort of ashamed of this child. They did not want to mention the fact that one of their children was mentally retarded. I am sure that all hon. members have at some time or other met a mother accompanied by a mentally retarded child who attempted to explain the situation by saying that the child was just not right. Today they are not ashamed to come out and say that the child is mentally retarded. That is accepted by everyone, without any stigma being attached to it.
The average person also realizes that the mentally ill can be treated and returned to society and they are accepted when they return to society. In addition, the average Canadian has developed a desire to assist the mentally ill patient and not to leave him in an isolated hospital. Rather they want to keep them in their own communities and, where possible, in their own homes and give them as much home treatment and comfort as possible. The average taxpayer has also exhibited an increased willingness to pay taxes for mental health grants. I am sure that most hon. members have at some time or other had someone approach them and urge increased mental health grants. This is an encouraging aspect of the picture of mental health. These grants have been increased and a number of personnel have received training under post-graduate scholarships awarded by the national research council.
The 120,000 members of the Canadian Mental Health Association have done a great

deal to bring about this change in attitude and we should be very grateful to them for their work. They can be assisted in this work by a continuation of television programs such as the one that was put on, I think, last May, which was a series of programs on mental health; I think the program was called "The Disordered Mind". In those programs mental treatment was illustrated. Quite frequently the program consisted of a psychiatrist leading a discussion and talking to a patient.
The resolution urges co-operation with the provinces and various interested organizations and groups in a number of aspects, including the extent of mental illness, its causes, treatment and the method of treatment. I am sure the hon. member knows it is sometimes difficult to obtain complete cooperation. Complete co-operation in a survey of the extent of mental illness would involve first a definition of mental illness. It is going to be very difficult to achieve co-operation in this field and in this aspect when there is no agreement on the definition of mental illness. Therefore, the first step should be to attempt to decide what is the line of demarcation between a mentally ill patient and what one would consider normal mental health. Likewise, on the causes of mental illness there is a great deal of controversy. We quite frequently hear from laymen in the field that the stress of modern life is the cause of the increased number of mentally ill patients.
