Yet as far back as 200 years ago doctors who were interested in mental health were stating at that time that the increased stress of life was the cause of mental illness, and we are still meeting that hazard and cause with actually very little basis to back up the statement.
Other schools of thought on the cause of mental illness will be most emphatic in stating that a disturbance in the body chemistry is the cause of mental upsets and there is a school of thought which is very successful in treating mental disturbances by chemical means. However, a survey could include a great deal of co-operation among the provinces.
The hon. member for Durham (Mr. Vivian) referred to a survey carried out by the province of Nova Scotia. I think the federal government has an opportunity to help in this regard. They should provide co-ordination, perhaps, rather than co-operation among the various provinces. It might be possible to get the various provinces interested to contribute a portion of their budgets to an organization to conduct two types of surveys, rural and urban. The survey could be carried out possibly in three urban and three rural areas, with all the provinces and the federal

government contributing to the survey. I think the quality of the survey would be much higher and it would be possible to obtain a greater number of qualified personnel for the survey and it could be used as an example of the co-operation between the provinces and the federal government.
There are numerous problems involved in the resolution. Probably one of the greatest is the acquiring of adequate specialized staff to treat mentally ill patients. Great progress has been made in this direction but the problem cannot be solved overnight. Various provincial governments are contributing to medical schools in their own provinces and here again we might get the provinces together to co-operate in a stepped-up program in training personnel.
One area in which co-operation could take place is in the rehabilitation of the mentally ill patient. This group would, of course, include alcoholics. One problem facing these unfortunate people is that quite often they are dismissed from their jobs. They undergo a course of treatment, are released from a treatment centre and then have difficulty in obtaining employment. If provincial rehabilitation branches, welfare departments and the national employment service could co-operate in obtaining employment for these people and at the same time provide a certain amount of supervision after they have started to work it would be most helpful.
Earlier in the discussion reference was made to the cost involved in implementing this resolution, and in that regard I believe the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) misinterpreted the remarks of the hon. member for Durham. It was my interpretation of his remarks that he was attempting to convey to the house that it is not the amount of money spent but rather the method used in research and treatment that is important. In other words, the same results can probably be achieved with $50 million as with $100 million. I think that is the point the hon. member for Durham was attempting to make.
The hon. member for Portage-Neepawa (Mr. Fairfield) mentioned the cost of research and the amounts we are spending on agriculture, defence and atomic research. The amounts spent are very large and they are spent to achieve certain purposes. The amount of money we spend on mental health should be measured against the cost of maintaining the patient in a hospital, providing treatment and also the loss of income to the nation.
Mental illness is not confined to any one income group or to any specific trade. It can affect people in all walks of life. I am sure that many of the people who sit in the galleries of the house have often wondered
Mental Illness Survey
whether some of the members of the house were not emotionally disturbed. An hon. member says "unbalanced", and that may be a much better description. I think it would be a sound financial proposition to spend more money on research and by so doing reduce the very high cost of hospitalization and at the same time increase national income.
Earlier I made reference to research and, along with other members who have spoken, emphasized its importance, but do not get the idea that research alone is the cure. For a number of reasons there must be some coordination and direction of research. Without this there will be a duplication of research groups. Perhaps I might illustrate the point by referring to a commission that was given to Dr. S. Bagnall, dean of dentistry, Dalhousie University. He was commissioned by the national research council to review and summarize the work on dental caries. Thousands of papers on dental caries were submitted to him and after reading them in a preliminary way he was forced to discard 2,000 papers as contributing nothing toward the knowledge of dental caries. I am sure that the same thing would apply to mental health. If one picks up any magazine one is almost certain to find on article on mental health. Many of these people referred to in these articles feel that they have contributed something to research and are looking for contributions toward their research.
I am happy to say that I support the principle of the resolution. I would prefer to see the word "co-ordination" used rather than "co-operation". However, if the hon. member achieves support for the principle of the resolution I am sure he will be happy and I am quite happy to support it.

speakeroldname: Mr. H. F. Jones (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I	should like to say a few words in support of the resolution which I think is a very excellent and timely one. For many years now people throughout the country have been seriously concerned about the cost in suffering and in non-productivity that mental illness causes and have been seeking ways in which they can grapple with this problem in the light of recent developments.
I think everyone in the house will agree that the Magna Carta as far as treatment on a comprehensive scale of those suffering from mental illnesses is concerned was established by the province of Ontario under its minister of health, Dr. Dymond, when on February
II	last he introduced into the Ontario house certain proposals dealing with a comprehensive approach to mental care in that province. The program that he then set forth was, I think, one of the highlights of many years of

Mental Illness Survey
endeavour. I should like to read a few words from what he said on that occasion because they lay the basis of modern treatment of mental illness. As found in the report of the debates of the Ontario legislature, Dr. Dymond had this to say:
The modern program of treatment has been based on the recognition of the patient's need for contact with well people, and for maintenance of his normal humanities. And, secondly, it is based on the patient's need to exercise whatever capacities for creativity, productivity and responsibility that he may have.
With these things in mind, the modern program of treatment and rehabilitation is aimed at early treatment, obtainable without legal formality or other impediment; treatment with as little disturbance of the patient's living pattern as possible, that is, without removal from job, home or com-muniy unless this is specifically indicated; restoration to normal activity in a normal environment as quickly and completely as possible, and the best use of residual abilities in those incompletely cured or partially disabled.
In some cases this may, and probably will, require special facilities and arrangements in the community; in other cases, special programs in the hospitals. Since the aim is to keep the patient in as close contact with his normal home and community environment as possible, a great deal of responsibility will devolve upon the community.
I think the resolution before us, Mr. Speaker, envisages in its wording some of the problems that have been pointed out at particular times and the necessity for grappling with these problems. As Dr. J. D. Griffin, the director general of the Canadian Mental Health Association has said, mental and emotional illness is the most difficult and most important health problem in Canada. Surely that is a view to which we can subscribe. It is not a simple problem and it has, I believe, to be attacked on a more comprehensive scale than it has been hitherto. I am advised that some of the difficulties the people operating in the mental health field have had to face, in addition to public apathy, have been the lack of co-ordination of research in its widest sense. For example, in the University of Saskatchewan, at the university hospital, much good work is being done in this particular field by Dr. McKer-racher and Dr. Hoffer, as well as other Saskatchewan names that immediately come to mind. These people are the leaders in what Dr. Osborne calls, unusually enough to some who have looked at the recent statements of psychiatrists, the traditional approach to treating mental illness. I gather from this that he is referring to the problems of body chemistry that are involved in the treatment of this condition.
It would seem to me, Mr. Speaker, that one of the fundamental problems, and a problem which is a public responsibility, is the realization for the necessity for action in this field. Action cannot be taken unless
there is public support, public co-operation, which is something to which the other speakers in this debate have referred.
Reference has been made, too, to the history of the public attitude toward mental and emotional disorders. I think that is changing now. I think the public attitude toward mental illness has been changing significantly, even in the last 10 years. This results not only from the endeavours of the professional people who are actively engaged with this problem, but of the various associations across the country who have devoted their time and efforts toward making the public aware of the value of supporting programs for mental health. Immediately there leaps to mind the tremendous work that has been done by the Canadian Mental Health Association, the provincial branches of that association, by the local visiting committees of the mental institutions and the professional people themselves in making the public aware of the necessity for coming to grips with this problem.
I should like to quote, if I may, just a paragraph or two from an article which Dr. J. D. Griffin wrote some time ago. He said:	!
At the present time nearly one half of all hospital beds in Canada are occupied by patients suffering serious mental illness. Careful surveys of sample populations have revealed that in addition to people who have been completely incapacitated by mental disorders, (estimated at more than 6 per 1,000 of the population) at least one in ten suffer from mental or emotional illness sufficiently serious to cause impairment of function amounting to 10 per cent or more. One Canadian study concludes that more than 370 per 1,000 of the adult population are currently impaired in this way.
You can see from these figures, Mr. Speaker, the seriousness of the problem and the necessity for its investigation, the necessity for public support to provide the means for treating mental and emotional illness. In one of the first speeches I made in the House of Commons after being re-elected in 1958 I referred to this problem of mental illness. I said, on that occasion, as reported on page 451 of Hansard for the 1958 session:
It has been emphatically recommended by those whose profession is the treatment of the mentally ill that, given the same standard of care as the physically ill, the mentally sick could go to the hospital with the expectation of returning to the community after treatment rather than remaining incarcerated for years or even for life. Mental sickness can be treated effectively. Much mental sickness can be treated effectively with very little hospitalization, provided the patient is afforded the same standard of care that is afforded to the physically sick. Such treatment could be provided in small hospitals or in the wards of general hospitals,-

And so on. I went on on that occasion to deal with some of the ways in which treatment of that kind could be advanced. The point I make is this: The statement I made on that occasion is supported by medical opinion. I have since received many letters commenting on that speeech and endorsing the views put forward at that time. This leads me to believe that perhaps we have now reached the time when we can move forward in a great national effort toward conducting a survey of the extent of mental illness, its causes, its problems and its methods of treatment as suggested in this house today by the hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. Macnaughton) as well as other members who have spoken. This is not a new request that is made, but perhaps at this time we have reached a situation where effect can be given to this request which has been made on so many occasions by the people who have been interested in mental health over the years.

I intend to say a few words on this resolution. When we are dealing with this field we are dealing with a field that affects everybody across Canada. The effect of this problem is felt in the homes, in the hospitals and in the schools right across Canada. I feel that we should turn to statistics to find out exactly what is the situation. They are often boring, perhaps, but a few figures will show what a tremendous number of mentally weak, ill and troubled people live in Canada today. In addition to the mentally weak and ill there is another horde of chronic complain-ers who remain chronically unwell for years and perhaps throughout their lifetime.
I recall how shocked I was a couple of years ago when 1 heard a speaker say that one out of every 10 babies born in Canada would spend some part of his or her lifetime in a mental institution. When we look around this chamber we can imagine what a problem that is, that one out of every 10 children born into this world will be in an institution some time before he dies or she dies.
Mental deterioration goes on and will increase. This problem will become bigger simply because we are today extending the span of man's life. People are living longer, and consequently we have more arteriosclerotic conditions and more senile deterioration.
It is a very important economic and social problem when you consider that 3 per cent of the babies born are mentally below par-it is estimated by some authorities that one person in 10 is either mentally unbalanced or has a serious problem of adjustment in his or her life. It is estimated
Mental Illness Survey
that here in Canada we have 300,000 psychopathic cases and another 500,000 partially incapacitated by nervous and psychic troubles. Those are things that I think will require a good, long look at.
Then add to this the fact that it is estimated that 2 per cent of our population is substandard in their intelligence. This gives us the astounding figure of 360,000 who cannot be counted on to support themselves. According to Dr. Cobb's figures-and I give them to you now-15 per cent of all school children in the United States need help; they need special attention. He also states that 15 per cent of all our students going to college need psychiatric counselling.
Then we must include epileptics, of course, in this group that need psychiatric help. There are some 80,000 to 90,000 epileptic people in Canada, or one half of one per cent of the population. Many of these are of course under proper treatment. They go to school and through university and they carry on in the business and professional life of this country without any problem. But some of those-approximately 7 per cent-will have to be admitted to hospitals for treatment.
A further 2 per cent of our population are chronic alcoholics, many of whom are under treatment at various times in mental institutions. Next we come to the drug addicts, who rightly come under this legislation. We find there are 5,000 to 6,000 drug addicts in Canada. Most of these are, of course, men.
Then we would probably have another 300,000 criminals either in institutions or out of institutions. These are divided, of course, among those who are first offenders and those who are not. I would class a man who is a repeated offender in our penitentiaries as a psychopath. That fellow of course should not be turned out; he should not be unloosed on the public until the psychiatrists have found that he is able to adjust himself. Some of them never are; but some of them will reach a stage of maturity which is later than the normal person reaches it. Of those fellows who are cured and go out, it is my experience from the people I have known that we do not have many of the first offenders repeat again, if they are not psychopaths.
Dr. Wolf has stated that from a study he made at least 50 per cent of those in general hospitals were suffering from emotional problems that were delaying their recovery and return to work. But I wonder how many of us stop to think what a costly problem that is today in the hospitals across Canada, with a figure of 50 per cent. Their stay in hospital is being prolonged. When Dr. Wolf looked at this problem, he came to the conclusion

Mental Illness Survey
that their stay in hospital was about three times as long as it was in the normal case. Of course, added to this is the problem of getting them back to work.
In brief, over 50 per cent of all patients seeing the medical profession today have an emotional, surgical or medical problem combined, or have only an emotional problem. Let me say that the emotions cause more illness, more absenteeism, more misery, more accidents than any other disease from which the human body suffers. I think that is a striking thing and must make a very great impact on us, when we consider that the emotional illnesses of this country are greater than all other problems of sickness that beset the human being.
Stresses and strains of modern living have added immeasurably to this problem of mental health. The mentally ill require not only care for this condition, but many of them also become physically sick through lack of hygiene, faulty diets and other causes. We know that there exists the problem of prenatal infection in the case of some little children who are born into the world below par. We know that if the mother contacts measles, or mumps or perhaps other viruses when she is carrying the baby, certain ill effects may arise.
I think this is a very important point, because today we have certain remedies; we can inoculate for some of these viruses-for measles, for example I think the time is very rapidly coming when we will be able to tackle this virus problem and see how much of the mental illness, or the mental retardation-let us put it that way-in those babies is due to some of those viruses infections hitherto untreated.
It does not require much thinking to go back to a few years ago, just before the advent of penicillin and antibiotics. Bacterial organisms used to beset us and we succumbed in many cases to these infections. All of us in this house can recall that pneumonia carried a mortality rate of one in five and that other illnesses-such as streptococcal infections, and so on were of the same order.
Yet today we have conquered these diseases with antibiotics. They have largely become diseases of the past, and my prediction would be that in a very few years we will have also completely conquered viruses. As a matter of fact, today we have almost got polio into a corner; we have almost conquered it and elimination is on the way. So I predict that in the next 10 years most of the viruses will be completely conquered and under control. My hope in saying this is that many of these defective children who are born into the world today will cease to be defective when these viruses are conquered.

I do not know of anything more distressing than to have a mother or a father see a little defective child come into their home. I do not know of anything sadder, after all the months they have looked forward to the coming of the little baby, than to have this happen.
I have a case in point now where the little baby is going to die; where the mother, at great inconvenience to herself, went through pregnancy only to find that her little child is going to pass on in the course of the next few weeks. These are things that strike right into the heart of the home, and anything we can do in the field of research that will accelerate the conquering of these viruses, so much the better for the people of this country.
Should the federal government do research in the field of viruses, including the effect of the common cold and its effect on the baby in utero? Should all mothers as part of their prenatal care, if they have not had measles, be immunized against its effects? What is the effect of the common cold virus on the foetus? Nobody knows. Nobody has done sufficient research on this question, so we do not know what the answer is. How can we tackle these problems so that, if possible, no baby shall be born into this world with a preventable defect. Yesterday we encountered the invading armies of the bacterial war. Our research workers have largely reduced this invasion to impotence. Today we encounter the invading armies of the viruses. They, too, must be met and conquered, and we are conquering them, quietly and gradually. Polio has been fought into a corner and contained; other viruses are being challenged, and tomorrow they must all be controlled. Perhaps, then, we shall see the numbers of these small children who have been born mentally defective lessened and, finally, disappear.
In Europe, and particularly in Great Britain, they have set up a registry of all mental cases for the purpose of compiling health statistics. They have analysed those substandard people and worked them into in many cases what they call sheltered industry. I know of nothing similar, to this in this country. Those people are put into work that they can do. They can produce, and they can keep themselves, and some of them even go out into the competitive field when they have learned their trade.
In conjunction with the Department of Justice, psychiatrists should study all criminals and categorize them as either psychopaths or non-psychopaths-this is done in a small way-because in my opinion only the psychopaths will be the repeaters, the nonpsychopath will be cured. The psychopaths, in general, will not be cured except as some

of them reach maturity, which they do much later than the average person, and may at that time shed sufficient of their psychopathic tendencies. I repeat that if they do not reach that maturity the psychopath, in my opinion should never be released from confinement.
There is need for the training of more research workers in this field, though I agree it is not as alluring and attractive as other branches of medicine-there is not the same allure to it as going in and snipping out an appendix. For hours one has to talk to these patients and understand their problems. There has to be understanding and sympathy if one Is to help these people. Nevertheless, in this field the greatest good can be done to the human race-to restore a man or woman to their homes, their businesses and their dignity when all was black and desolate; to restore faith and confidence to the greatest creation of our Lord is, indeed, the highest function of human skill.
In conclusion, let me say that the province of Ontario has one of the finest health departments to be found anywhere in the world and the federal government should aid and assist the province in this way and in no way take over or duplicate any of the work that Is now being done in this field. It is unnecessary to have a lot of duplication because, as we know, there is a certain law which says that activities of this kind produce more and more bureaucracy without getting to the root of the problem at all. This might well even be a part of the mental and emotional frustrations from which people now suffer.

As several hon. members have said, we are grateful to the hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. Mac-naughton) for presenting this resolution today because it gives hon. members in all quarters of the house an opportunity to bring before the minister their concern about a problem which, I know, concerns him and engages his attention. In presenting this resolution, the hon. member for Mount Royal is following in the tradition of the former member for St. Lawrence-St. George, who as an officer of the Canadian Mental Health Association and as a member of this house caused our attention to be directed from time to time to various aspects of this problem.
This is a matter which cuts across party lines and gives us an opportunity to join together in the pursuit of an objective which has no party interest as such. I am sure that the statistics given to us, particularly by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) and the hon. member for Simcoe East (Mr. Rynard) speak for themselves. None will
Mental Illness Survey
deny the seriousness of this problem, a problem which has taken on an accelerated character largely, as the last speaker said, because of the nature of the society in which we live, a society which is becoming more and more industrialized with the result that on this and other accounts stresses are produced which add to the incidence of mental illness in one form or another. I do not propose to deal with the statistics, except to say, as one who had ministerial responsibility in the general field of health policy on federal account, that I recognize at once that there has been no exaggeration, generally speaking, today in stating the character of the problem in our country.
In analysing what we must do about it we have to bear in mind the advice just given by the hon. member for Simcoe East and recognize that under the British North America Act functions have been allocated to the two senior levels of government. This is not in any way stated by myself or by anyone else in order to excuse the federal government from bearing its proper share of responsibility. There is a proper sphere of responsibility for the federal government in this matter. That responsibility lies largely in seeing to it that there is as wide a distribution of health facilities made available to all Canadians as possible. The federal government also has the responsibility of seeing to it, in co-operation with the provinces that whatever projects the latter undertake are co-ordinated in such a way as to meet the first requirement and at the same time to provide as useful a service as possible.
I well remember when the national health program was introduced in 1948 receiving a wire from the leader of the Conservative party in the province of Prince Edward Island at that time-his name escapes me and perhaps someone would help me to recall it-
Mr. MacMillan.

I thank the Prime Minister. I was referring to Dr. MacMillan whose work in the field of public health in my judgment was most outstanding. He wired me to say that at last he felt that his province would be given the necessary funds to enable it to begin at long last, particularly in the field of mental health, a program that up until that time it had not been possible to undertake there. I was greatly encouraged by the wire from Dr. MacMillan whom I did not know at that time. He later became one of my closest friends and a collaborator on a very constructive level. As a matter of fact, shortly after that I went down to Prince Edward Island, and at the suggestion of the then premier in whose government he did

Mental Illness Survey not serve, I was shown around the mental institutions and facilities that existed in that province.
I do not exaggerate when I say that the funds made available by the federal government at that time certainly came not too soon. The crowded conditions in a particular mental health institution in that province were not such as to make Canadians feel proud of what had been the record of achievement. I am not saying this by way of criticism of any government or province, but it was just not possible for many provinces to undertake the kind of work that had to be done in the mental health field unless the federal government made available moneys which some of the provinces at that time simply did not have at their disposal. I am sure that is still the case with respect to some of the provinces in other respects as well and perhaps even in this field of mental health.
The role of the federal government in this particular is clear. It is to assist the provinces in carrying out their responsibility in the field of health care. The latter have the executory departments. They have the necessary access, because they are closer to the people in a way that the federal government can never hope to be. It has never been suggested in recent periods that the federal government should undertake a responsibility in this regard which can best be discharged by the provinces. What has been suggested is that in our effort to raise the levels of health care all over Canada, the federal government should use its greater resources to provide assistance which the provinces themselves can not always provide and at the same time through policies of co-ordination to provide for as uniform a standard of health care as is possible in our country.
I believe that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Monteith) is now co-operating with the provinces in this particular field as well as in others. There has been no suggestion by the hon. member for Mount Royal or any other speaker that that is not the case. What is urged in this resolution is that:
-the government should consider the advisability of co-operating with the provincial authorities and such professional and other groups as may be interested, in making a national survey of the extent of mental illness, its causes, problems and methods of treatment.
There has been some suggestion, notably by the hon. member for Durham (Mr. Vivian), that the precise terms used by the hon. member for Mount Royal were not perhaps as accurate as they should be. Possibly he was thinking of the inclusion of the words "its causes" in the resolution, I do not know.


In any event as the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa (Mr. Fairfield) pointed out, the intention behind this resolution is clear, and it is the intention that counts and not any over-statement of the problem or failure to properly pinpoint it.
The question is whether or not the time has come for the federal government to cooperate with the provinces in making a national survey of mental illness. It will be recalled, that when the national health program was announced in May of 1948, the federal government of that day announced that for the first time the federal government would undertake to make grants on an unconditional basis to the provincial governments, without any strings attached to assist them in their general program of health care. It was to cover specifically public health, cancer control, tuberculosis control, mental illness, hospital construction, medico-scientific research and professional training. Some years afterward three other grants were added without in any way affecting the basic grants I have just enumerated.
It is significant that the mental health grant was to rise after a period from the original $4 million to $7 million a year and since that time, as we were reminded today by the hon. member for Durham, that amount has risen from $7 million, I believe, to $9 million or thereabouts.
Included in the original grant was a grant to do the very thing which the hon. member for Mount Royal is asking this house to do again, some 12 years later. The sum of $600,000 was provided by the federal government in May of 1948, to assist the provinces in making a survey of their health needs generally, including mental illness. In addition the provinces were given this money to undertake by themselves surveys in each of the 10 provinces which would give them and the federal government an opportunity of knowing exactly what were the facilities available to the various provincial departments of health to enable them to discharge a responsibility assigned to them by custom under the constitution.
The information that was made available as a result of these surveys is open to any government and any individual in this country. I am sure the minister will agree that the information given to the health workers and governments all over this country particularly in the mental health field was extremely valuable. It confirmed in statistical form the deplorable state of mental illness in Canada at that time. It pointed out the great shortage of psychiatrists and of personnel equipped with medical training to meet this problem, the lack of personnel generally, the

lack of institutional facilities in many provinces. It gave to health workers and governments all over the country an opportunity of making an assessment so that they could at long last in a co-operative way begin to tackle this extremely serious problem.
Twelve years have now elapsed. It seems to me that it is reasonable to suggest it might be useful in the face of the situation as it now exists that we should perhaps make sure once again that we have a clear picture of the problem in Canada. It is not that we think it is any more serious than in any other comparable country, but in our effort to tackle this problem we want to make sure precisely what is its nature.
I am sure that the minister will be able to say that in the interval, during the time that he has been responsible for the department, as was the case when I had that responsibility, there have been frequent meetings with the provincial governments, notably with the dominion council of health, and more particularly with the heads of the mental health divisions of the various provincial governments. I am sure the meetings have been held here at Ottawa with the federal government. As a result, the minister and other responsible officials in government throughout Canada have at their disposal now the kind of information which is called for in this resolution. I would be the last to challenge the minister in that particular. I know that this continuous collaboration with the provinces in the field of health is valuable. Perhaps there is no area of intergovernmental activity in Canada where the collaboration is as intimate and as valuable as in the field of health. But I would question whether those biennial, or annual conferences, or those continuous contacts really will cover the situation.
I am asking the minister to accept this resolution. It does not impose on him an obligation to carry out a survey, but it does call upon him to give consideration to the advisability, in co-operation with the provinces, of carrying out a survey. Could he not accept the resolution on those conditions and accordingly give consideration, either in his own department or in conjunction with his own colleagues before or after the meeting of the dominion council of health, as to whether or not the time has come when this kind of survey should be undertaken. There can be no question about the cost because money is now available for this purpose. We were told by the hon. member for Durham that out of some $77 million appropriated by parliament since 1948 in the field of mental health, only some $50 million has been expended. When the minister
Mental Illness Survey
speaks I am sure he will indicate that the moneys allocated for this present fiscal year have not all been utilized. In any event, it is possible by a transfer of vote to arrange for the necessary moneys to be paid entirely by the federal government or in conjunction with the provincial governments. That can be arranged if it is decided that this survey is now necessary.
I support this resolution along the lines I have indicated, and I would hope that the minister would accept it in the sense that I have suggested, namely that in a matter of this kind it would be difficult for the government not to agree to consider the advisability of co-operating with the provincial authorities and with professional and other groups in making a national survey of this problem.
The survey of 1948 did point up the need. Since that time many hundreds of new health workers have been added to provincial mental health divisions. More personnel of all kinds have been added to the mental institutions carried on by the provinces. In this regard, in commenting on the statement of the last speaker, I should simply say there really is no opportunity for duplication of effort in this particular field.
The federal government does not undertake to operate mental institutions. That function is properly left to the provinces. The only area where there could be duplication, I think, would be in the field of research because, as the hon. member for Durham did point out, before the national health program was announced in 1948 some of the provinces, notably the province of Ontario, were doing some research in this field. But the collaboration between the two senior levels of government is such that I think even in the field of research the danger of duplication is not great. The hon. member for Simcoe East, was not unwise in calling our attention to this danger.
I mentioned that moneys originally appropriated for this work were not fully expended in the first year and, as a matter of fact, were not fully expended in subsequent years. The main reason for that was that there were not enough health workers or people trained in this field to do the job. One of the first things that had to be done with the moneys provided by the federal government was to train people so that the provinces would have the necessary skills to do the job. That had to be done then, and it continues to be done today.
With the funds that were provided by the federal government general hospitals were given the opportunity of establishing psychiatric units where, as the hon. member for Vancouver East said, much has been

Mental Illness Survey
done. Up until 1956, the last year for which I have figures, some 44 hospitals in Canada had established psychiatric units with help that had been given to them by the federal government. Mental health clinics were established practically for the first time. There were in 1957, and I am sure the minister can point to much higher figures today, over 130 out-patient services and mental health clinics where individuals were able to go, individuals who were suffering from the kind of emotional disturbance which the hon. member for Simcoe East discussed a few moments ago. They were able to go there and be diagnosed. In many instances they were sent to a mental institution; in other instances they were treated early, or the nature of the diagnosis indicated that they did not need the kind of more fundamental treatment provided for in an institution. The number of psychiatrists, the number of psychologists, the number of nurses, the number of social workers and other professional mental health personnel who have received training under mental health grants is great. I would not be surprised if today it runs into a figure of close to 4,000. In 1956 it was around 2,000.
The number of bursary holders and others doing specialized training so that they would receive adequate and rapid training is large. The number of people in our universities strained our training facilities beyond the capacity of the universities to provide them. I suspect that that situation has improved considerably since.
Mention has been made of research. It would be wrong to say that the only area of assistance to be given in this field is in the field of research. That would be wrong because the amount of institutional care, the amount of help to institutions that is required, the amount of statistical assessment of this problem alone is something that is, as the minister I am sure will indicate, of the greatest importance. But great assistance has been given to mental health research.
When I think of the work that is being done in the Allan memorial institute in Montreal under Dr. Cameron, and the fact that this institution would not have been able to carry on its work but for assistance given by the federal government over the years under the plan now administered by the Minister of National Health and Welfare, I cannot help but join with others in recognizing the importance of research. Great benefits have been derived from this research and will continue. But this is only one aspect of the problem.
The minister will have the support of the house in the consideration that he will give to this matter. In the spirit in which we have

approached this problem today, I suggest to him that the desire of all of us is to make sure that everything that possibly can be done by the federal government in this field is being done. I am not suggesting it is not being done, but we would be assured in that regard if the minister would accept this resolution, if he would agree to consider the advisability of determining now whether a large national survey along the lines of that undertaken in 1948 should be repeated. The minister would find that the house would be prepared to give the fullest support to him in such a decision.
It is not a question, as the hon. member for Durham suggested-and I am sure he did not mean to suggest this-that we recognize that this is the only health problem. Of course there are other health problems, some of them of the greatest magnitude. Not much is to be gained by saying which is the greater. The amount of money and effort that yet have to go into research into heart diseases is very great and, as I have suggested on another occasion, I think there is a great deal that can be done by us in that field that is not being done. But we are now dealing with one field, a field which challenges us as few other problems at the moment do.
No one could listen to the hon. member for Simcoe East say a few moments ago that 50 per cent of the cases that come before general practitioners have to do with mental health or with surgery without feeling that if that is the statistic then the challenge of the problem is one that is as great as any problem that has ever been put before us. We are not flinching with regard to our responsibilities in the matter of national defence and other responsibilities that attend this parliament, but in the face of that statistic I am sure the minister will find it desirable to accept this resolution and in doing so he will receive our full support.

Mr. Speaker, after listening to the debate this afternoon I am quite certain I could not add anything substantial to what has been said by previous speakers. If anyone is interested in reading about his activities in that respect and in other directions, he would be well advised to spend three or four dollars to purchase a book written by Mrs. D. G. Steeves, a former member of the legislature of British Columbia, entitled "The Compassionate Rebel", which deals with the activities of the father of the hon. member for Vancouver East.

Mr. Speaker, many tensions have been imposed on mankind in our western civilization, today. Many experts have taken part in the debate on the resolution this afternoon. I should like, as previous speakers have done, to take this opportunity of congratulating the hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. Macnaughton) upon putting this resolution before us. As has been said before we are talking about an extremely important subject. Statistics have been put on record this afternoon to illustrate the gravity of this problem.
It is easy to understand when a man goes into a doctor's office-and I repeat that I do not speak as an expert but, unfortunately, I have had some experience with this problem as it has related to friends of mine- with a broken arm or a broken leg, but it is not quite as easy to recognize when the spirit or the mind is about to be broken. The revolution that has taken place in the field of psychiatry during the past years has resulted in such things as the electric shock treatment, drug treatment and hypnotism. As the hon. member for Mount Royal said, our institutions are no longer referred to as asylums. We now see, too, that these institutions have two doors, not only a door

Mental Illness Survey
going in but a door coming out. It has become generally recognized that people suffering from mental illness can often be completely rehabilitated. It has also become generally recognized, Mr. Speaker, that we can talk openly about mental illness. Certainly we should be able to do so because, as I said before, statistics have been placed before us which show that a great percentage of people are suffering from mental illness.
I should like to join with previous speakers this afternoon in bringing the importance of this resolution before the house. I should like to join with other speakers who have this afternoon brought this matter to the attention of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Monteith). I am sure it has been brought to his attention before, and I am sure that this most important resolution will meet with his complete commendation.

I should like to join with other members in congratulating the hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. Macnaughton) upon bringing this resolution before the house. This is the first time I have seen a resolution presented by the opposition meet with such whole hearted approval from every member of the house. I am very proud that this unanimity has been indicated on this most important subject. My mother was a nurse in an asylum in Toronto when she came to this country about 75 years ago. During my childhood I heard the problems of the mentally ill discussed. This made a great impression upon me and I have followed the discussions of this important subject with a great deal of sympathy.
In April of 1939 a promising young man joined my firm. Six months afterwards he went to an institution with t.b. About a year later he returned and was going along fine but evidently, as a result of this t.b., he was sent to a mental institution about eight months later. This was about 1942 or 1943, and he is still there. Within the last month or so I have received word that this man will shortly be released from that institution. When he was committed to this place his case was regarded as hopeless. However, modern research and the development of new techniques in connection with mental health have resulted in the cure of this young man and it looks as if he will be returning to society to perform a useful function again.
I must say that I appreciate the work that went into the presentation by the hon. member for Mount Royal and the statistics that he presented to us this afternoon. They were most enlightening to me. I have not followed the subject as closely as he has. I have a great many friends in the Canadian Mental Health Association, and I know something of

the time they have given voluntarily to work in this field. I am sure, because I have discussed the subject with him, the minister is well aware of these problems. However, it does take time to reach a solution.

Mr. Speaker, before we
recessed at six o'clock I was telling the story of a young employee of mine who had been committed to an institution 17 years ago and after four or five years in this mental institution had been given up as a hopeless case. But in the last two months, through research and modern methods of treatment, there is a possibility that this young man will be returning to his wife and child after 17 years.
Quite recently the minister authorized a grant for a clinic in my riding, and I may say that it was through no pressure by the member. But I think the establishment of these clinics to which local people can come for treatment is an excellent move.
I am a bit of a farmer. I was raised on the farm and have gone back to it in the last 24 years. I have seen the money that has been spent by provincial and federal governments and by the farmer to improve livestock. Millions and millions of dollars have been spent to improve livestock. I think that is one thing that we should be very, very proud of in Canada; the livestock that we have on our farms today compares with any anywhere in the world. We should be very proud of that fact.
But on the other hand we allow mentally deficient people to be joined in matrimony and raise children who will be a liability and cause heart-rending situations for all time to these people. I know I am on a delicate subject; I know this is a religious subject. But I say that today, when you consider the number of mentally deficient children, we should do something about it. I think the church should adopt a more positive attitude toward this matter. The hon. member for Simcoe East (Mr. Rynard) is also one of the leading Holstein breeders in this country, and I think he has the largest

children's mental hospital in Ontario in his community. I think he will support me in this point of view.
I was approached more than five years ago to join the directorate of our local hospital, in a community of about 4,000 people. We had a hospital there with 54 beds. We raised sufficient money to more than double that number of beds; we now have 117 beds. That addition to the hospital was only opened four years ago, and today we are confronted with increasing the number of beds to 300. Why is this? It is because a great many of those beds are occupied by people who have no reason to be there; they are there because there is no other place in which they can be treated. I think this is a great waste of money, because we found in building that addition to the hospital that it cost $15,000 per bed. I am sure that a mentally deficient patient can be treated in a building that does not cost that amount of money.
Today in our community we are confronted with a $9 million hospital program. Early in September I spoke to my good friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker) and asked him to put before the government the idea of a winter works program of hospital construction. I did this because I know that all across this country we really need hospitals. I think the minister should seriously consider this suggestion.
I have also observed in our community that this same hospital that has long been used for t.b. patients is not filled. I am wondering why this hospital could not be utilized for the treatment of mentally deficient people. I also believe that Sunnybrook hospital is not filled. I think that there also we could probably utilize some of the beds that are available.
I will not be a party to asking the federal government to do everything. I think that is one of the great faults in Canada today. If any catastrophe, small or large, happens in a community, the first question asked is, "What is the government going to do about it?" We have become too dependent on the federal government. We look to the federal government to solve all problems. I believe it is a good thing for any community to help solve these matters itself.

It gives me a great deal of pleasure to support this resolution, not only because of its timeliness and importance but also because of the high regard in which I hold its sponsor, the hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. Macnaughton), after serving under him on committees of public accounts for the last three years.
In Canada in recent years there has been an increased awareness of the problem of mental disease particularly among certain segments of our society. I think perhaps the experience of the small city in which I live may be interesting to some hon. members. Just within the last few months Barrie has formed a branch of the Canadian Mental Health Association. The sponsors of this

Mental Illness Survey
branch were members of the women's university club of that city. But who were the first members of its board of directors? I think this is very interesting and significant. They included the family court judge, a number of doctors, social service workers, a clergyman, teachers, probation officers and lawyers, particularly lawyers whose practice fell in the field of domestic relations, and in small centres most lawyers do have to undertake considerable work in this direction. These are the people who see the damage caused by the lack of treatment of mental illness and, therefore, they are the people who are most interested in improving the present situation.
The hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) referred to a statement made by the hon. member for Simcoe East (Mr. Rynard) and used the words, if I quote him correctly, "if that is a statistic". I think that here the hon. member, perhaps inadvertently, put his finger on one of the greatest problems of mental ill health and one which is referred' to in the wording of the resolution itself where the need for a national survey of the extent of mental illness is pointed out. The extent of mental illness is one of the things about which there is a great deal of ignorance. It is very hard to measure, because there has always been a certain stigma attached to a person being committed to a mental institution, and a certain stigma attached also to the family-old wives tales about heredity and so on. For this reason, a great deal of mental illness has gone unnoticed. If this resolution were to result in nothing more than the production of a reasonable set of statistics it would, in my opinion, have accomplished a great deal.
Too often, also, when mental illness occurs local facilities are inadequate or else there is no local treatment available. Committal to a hospital is an important step for the family to take. Sometimes, I have found, doctors are reluctant to suggest treatment. The whole field surrounding the early stages of mental ill health is one which has been hidden away from the public gaze; the public has not been aware of it, and accordingly we have not been able to confront it properly or provide a means of lessening the problem.
The resolution also speaks of a survey of methods of treatment. Co-ordination in this field' is most important. A great deal has already been done in all parts of Canada, but I should like to refer to my own province for a minute. I think members on both sides of the house would profit very much from reading the debates of the Ontario legislature as recorded in the record for 1959 at page 284 and following pages where the Hon. M. B. Dymond, minister of health, recites the very

considerable progress which has been made in the treatment of mental ill health in Ontario both inside and outside hospitals.
As a practising country lawyer I have always felt when these problems come to my desk, as they do come to many country lawyers, that the greatest need is for a psychiatric clinic near at hand where a person could get treatment ini the early stages, possibly exploratory treatment which would define the limits of his mental problems. It is very difficult to get such treatment. The psychiatric clinics in the cities are so occupied and their waiting lists are so long that very often people cannot afford' to take the necessary time to go down and await such treatment. It is for this reason I am particularly interested in what Mr. Dymond, said as reported on page 287, and I should like to quote this from his remarks:
Perhaps one of the most outstanding achievements in this whole field of mental health has been the opening of two day-care centres in 1958, one at the Toronto psychiatric hospital, the other at the Ontario hospital in Cobourg.
I may say I should like to see these centres opened at locations away from presently existing hospitals where institutional care is provided. I should like to see more of them opened in cities and towns where no mental hospital exists. I continue:
It is worthy of note, and I believe that this house should take a good deal of pride in this knowledge that, as far as we can ascertain, this unit at Cobourg is the first such centre in a predominantly rural area on this continent.
I should like to make a few remarks about daycare centres.
I believe this is very interesting. I continue:
Many patients require more attention than can be provided in a mental health clinic, but do not need to be admitted to a hospital. These are the severe psycho-neurotics or those showing early signs of psychotic disorder. Some of them, for example-middle-aged women, alone during the day-are much better when in the company of the family during the evening or on week ends.
To help these people, the day-care centres were begun. They offer a full range of diagnostic and treatment services offered by the mental hospital or psychiatric unit with the exception of 24-hour care or supervision.
He goes on to say, too, that in the case of discharged patients:
Experience has shown that many patients who appear well in hospital have great difficulty adjusting to community life. We believe the day-care centres can be of much value in forming a bridge between the protected environment of the hospital and a full, independent life in the community. In other words, we think if patients who have just left the hospital know there is such a place to which they can go for advice and reassurance when home and community living begin to bother them, there will be fewer readmissions, and even the original stay in hospital may be shortened.

I think that is a very worth-while start. It is something that ought to be and can and will be extended. It seems to me as a layman having very little real knowledge of mental disorders that many people who are mentally ill can be helped greatly by just having the opportunity of talking to qualified psychiatrists and people who have training in that line.
The hon. member for York North (Mr. Cathers) mentioned that he did not want to see the federal government have the responsibility for everything. I might call as a witness in his behalf Dr. J. E. Gilbert, former chief of the mental health division of the Department of National Health and Welfare in Ottawa, by quoting from his article which appeared in the January, 1960 issue of the Medical Services Journal. Speaking of mental illness, Dr. Gilbert said:
Illness of this-or for that matter any other- kind is a community responsibility, andi recent years have seen the growth of a new concept in which there is a reorientation of mental health services towards community care, and away from hospital care-*
Finally I would express the hope that when a survey is made it will deal particularly with the question of tranquillizers and similar drugs and their effect on mental health. As laymen we are continually confused by articles on the subject presenting conflicting views. One month we see an article reprinted from this or that medical journal saying that tranquillizers are wonderful and a sure cure for this or that malady and a month later another article appears in a rival magazine saying that tranquillizers are no good and ought to be thrown in the garbage. I believe this point could very well be covered in such a survey.
In closing I wish to say it is a great pleasure to speak in support of a motion that has received such wide general commendation throughout the house.
