It is because I wish to associate myself with those speakers who have preceded me and congratulate them upon their treatment of this subject which has become so important to our nation in recent years. I, too, should like to compliment the hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. Macnaughton) on bringing in this resolution. It reflects the thinking of this hon. gentleman and is certainly a tribute to the way in which he contributes to this house.
It has certainly been more than interesting this afternoon to hear the part that those hon. members who are doctors by profession have taken in this discussion, to hear
Mental Illness Survey
the fund of knowledge they are able to contribute concerning research in the various and may facets of this important subject, to understand how seriously all branches of the medical profession view this unfortunate and perhaps all too frequent occurrence among the population today. With our increased tempo of living we can well appreciate that this problem will perhaps increase rather than decrease in magnitude. The tensions and other causes that contribute to this unhappy state of the mental attitude are growing instead of decreasing. It is therefore interesting and highly gratifying to hear from the doctors who have spoken today representing various ridings about the extent to which the medical profession is working assiduously toward solving this national problem.
I was greatly interested to hear the contribution of the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin), a former minister of national health and welfare, and to learn from his wide knowledge of this subject the steps which that hon. member believes we should take to follow a course that would help solve the problem. I personally had no idea whatever of the degree to which Canada is infected by this unfortunate state of affairs until just recently in the riding of Kent there commenced the erection, now almost complete, of a hospital with some 1,200 beds to house only children afflicted by mental disorders. This hospital is to be used as a centre to see if something can be done to help these children in a manner that will prepare them to return to the world as citizens capable of playing their useful part.
A 1,200 bed hospital, of course, is one of great magnitude. We thought that the provincial government with the assistance of the federal government was perhaps thinking far into the future in providing this facility. Unfortunately I must confess that it now appears that this hospital must shortly be greatly increased in size in order to accommodate the many patients whose applications have already been received.
The resolution before us calls for the setting up of a co-operative body of provincial and federal authorities to make a national survey into mental illness, its causes, problems and methods of treatment. I am sure that this in itself constitutes a tremendous challenge to the medical research council that this government has set up independent of the national research council. It presents a problem to that body that calls for a tremendous effort on its part, a problem encompassing a scope perhaps unheard of in this type of research.
It is gratifying today to see the degree of interest in the subject of mental health taken

Mental Illness Survey
by hon. members. One of the reasons I am so proud to take part in this discussion arises from the fact that there has been absent from our discussion in this chamber this afternoon any trace of partisan politics. We have witnessed instead an honest and sincere desire on the part of hon. members in all parts of the house to see if something cannot be done about this unfortunate problem. This non-partisan attitude makes me very proud indeed to be associated with this hon. house.
I was also very interested in the remarks made by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) when he spoke of the noble and worth-while work of a nursing home set up by a few individuals. It was not a problem that appeared just at the spur of the moment. As the hon. member pointed out, the nursing home was eventually taken over by the government and is in operation today. Surely when we see the work of a few individuals bear fruit in this way, perhaps it would be well for the provincial governments, in conjunction with the federal government, to take another look at the very fine nursing homes in Ontario and I am sure in other provinces as well to see whether under proper supervision much more of this work could not be carried out so that patients could be taken out of the very crowded institutions and put in an atmosphere which would contribute very much to the road back and aid them to become once more the citizens that we need in this vast country today. You will appreciate, Mr. Speaker, that one of our great needs in Canada today is more citizens. Certainly if we can take them out of institutions and place them once more in a position where they can contribute their small part we shall be doing a service that we shall all be proud of.
I should like to add my name to those of many others who are sincerely endeavouring to find a method by which this large problem can be attacked in a concerted way, and I hope we shall be successful in opening up the new vistas which the new drugs and treatment make possible. I have no hesitation in saying that I most heartily endorse the resolution introduced by the hon. member for Mount Royal.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to associate myself with those who have spoken in suppport of the resolution introduced by the hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. Macnaughton). It is a worth-while resolution and should be accepted. In speaking to the resolution, I should like to say that this investigation should embrace the causes of mental illness, the problems that are effected by it and the treatment of it. The investigation should be organized in that order. As we

all know, mental health comes under the jurisdiction of the provinces. However, it should be organized by the provinces in co-operation with the federal government.
As to the causes of mental illness, there are many. There are congenital causes which can be inherited, illnesses can be caused by birth injuries, and some may be due to environment. They can also be due to the illnesses of the parents, which are not their fault or which might be their fault. The cause may be alcoholism, drug addiction, physical illness, social disease or other causes. Children who come from such homes as I have mentioned should not be blamed. It could not possibly be their fault and the children should not have to suffer for the sins of the parents. Treatment should be available to all these people. Investigation should be made into treatment that would cure them.
I understand that the line between those who are mentally retarded or mentally handicapped and those who are not is very thin indeed. It should not be impossible for the medical profession to find ways and means of solving those problems. The problems looking toward a cure are, of course, educational, constitutional and financial. However, the financial problem should not be a matter of too great moment because if the governments fulfil their obligations the financial strain or stress should not be too much on the private individual.
The matters of treatment could, of course, embrace mental hygiene. So far as retarded children are concerned there is always a way of training them. There are certain people with cerebral palsy and other afflictions who can get training and treatment throughout their lives that will equip them to do certain things, even though the wall between retardation and intelligence is not too great. Of course, for adults there are the mental institutions and general hospitals. As I said before, there should be very little difficulty in the medical profession in finding ways and means of overcoming the defects that these unfortunate people suffer from.
In conclusion, I, along with a great many others here today, would like to recommend to the minister that this resolution be accepted and approved. It would give me great pleasure to see this happen.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to add my concurrence to that of other hon. members who have spoken I should just like to comment on three specific matters. We have had many statistics today in connection with the increase in mental health. In connection with that I should like to read from Resume, the Canadian Mental Health Association magazine

of February, 1960. I refer to a projection for broadcast by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation network by Dr. J. D. Griffin, general director of the Canadian Mental Health Association. He said:
In 1980 we can expect there will be about 125,000 Canadian citizens in mental hospitals at any one time, compared with about 75,000 now. The stress and strain of life will continue to shatter-at least partially-the mental health of about 10 per cent to 15 per cent of the population, perhaps a little higher percentage than is the case now. The stresses will certainly be different however. The anxieties and tensions will be more global and less local in nature. But the impact on both collective and individual personality will be roughly the same, with the incidence of casualties-stress casualties- slightly higher.
All this will happen unless we do something in the next five to 10 years to reverse the trend. We desperately need a stepped-up research program.
These problems become much more real when they are closer to home. We have heard today how, over the years, medicine has conquered many diseases. In the town of Gravenhurst which is in the Muskoka district where I live there has been a hospital for tuberculosis since the last century. For a great many years people suffering from tuberculosis were sent to that institution. We are very happy to learn that medicine has now conquered tuberculosis and while there are still some cases the incidence of the disease has gone down so greatly that it was found necessary earlier this year to close the great Muskoka hospital for tuberculosis. However, it was taken over immediately as a mental hospital for retarded children. The Orillia hospital has been terribly overcrowded and the Muskoka hospital has now become a branch of the Orillia hospital. The situation is becoming so much clearer to us when we see what has happened in the field of medicine. We hope that within a very few years, and the fewer the better, medicine will discover the causes of and find cures for mental disease.
If the resolution before us today draws the attention of members of the house, the Canadian people and the government to the problem and if research is stepped up the day will definitely be hastened when mental illness will be cut back and it will then be our lot in Muskoka to find some other use for the great hospital there. I am sure no one will be sorry if that day comes.
The children who were moved into the Muskoka hospital are not mentally retarded in the sense that they are subnormal but rather they are children who are retarded because of defects they have had from birth. We in our district wonder whether such disabilities could not be discovered before birth and whether some cure, as has been mentioned by the medical members who have
Mental Illness Survey
spoken today, could not be found. If research can do it, it will certainly be a great thing for the country.
The second point I want to mention has to do with a member of the house who unfortunately is not in his seat today. I refer to the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Anderson). Many of us can do something by standing up and making a speech but the hon. member for Waterloo South has taken a very great interest in mentally retarded children and in recent years organized a drive to establish a school for such children in his home town of Galt. The school, known as the William Anderson school for retarded children, is now in operation, and it will stand as a tribute to his great humanitarian efforts.
The final subject on which I wish to speak has to do with mental illness as it relates to juveniles and adults who are guilty of criminal offences or delinquency of some sort. This matter was touched upon briefly this afternoon. We find that there is a continual increase in juvenile delinquency in Canada and the use of corrective measures does not seem to help. It seems that we will have to take preventive measures in order to help these people who are erring by studying their mental processes and behaviour patterns and why they do certain things. It is a most important subject in which I became interested a few years ago. I certainly think that such a study of the behaviour of persons, either adult or juvenile, who act differently from the rest of the population would be a great advantage. For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I think the resolution before us deserves support.

Mr. Speaker, I seldom take part in debates because other members cover the ground or bring up the points that come to my mind. However, I could not help but feel today that this is a most important matter and I think the hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. Mac-naughton) deserves a great deal of commendation for bringing it forward. Whether the debate will result in more money being set aside for this purpose may be questionable but I think there is one thing it has done. It has emphasized the point mentioned by the mover in his opening remarks, that mental illness has been something about which people have whispered and have not faced up to. When I look back a few years to the period prior to the second world war I recall that this seemed to be the attitude of most pepole in my area. The words "mental illness" were not used. It was said that a person was crazy and such cases were considered beyond redemption.
I remember that during the war I had a lot of experience with the medical people

Mental Illness Survey
over a period of two years and I learned a great deal. For the first time I became convinced that mental illness was similar to many other illnesses, that it was something that could be treated and that we should face up to it. People were learning more about it and medical science was commencing to do something about it. Since the second world war great strides have been made and governments, medical societies and other organizations who have had a part in such progress deserve a lot of credit. As a result I believe that the majority of the people of Canada are prepared to look upon mental illness today with a different attitude from what was formerly the case.
To me there are many phases of mental illness although they may all be classed under that heading. Medical men talk about mental illness in terms which I as a layman do not understand, but regardless of what terms are used it is a sickness of the mind and body which I believe can be cured in a great many cases and helped in others. What is required is the sympathetic understanding of the public at large with sufficient backing from all governments and medical associations to support research in this regard as much as possible having in mind the doctors and scientists that are available.
I was very much impressed with the speech of the hon. member for Durham (Mr. Vivian) today because I heard the very words he uttered today from medical men at a hospital at which I was stationed more than eight years ago. The hon. member said that we cannot force this thing, that it takes time but that we must keep abreast of research. I think research is the key. I think that in the last few years the government has been doing very well in supplying the money that was required. If more money is required, if it can be used economically, if we have the staff and we can provide the personnel without injurious effect on the work that has been undertaken, then I am prepared to vote more money.
I feel that that is what the hon. member for Mount Royal had in mind when he framed this resolution. Although the wording of the resolution is rather broad-if I had drawn it I would not have worded it that way-I take no exception to it because it brings this subject to public attention and to the attention of the members of the House of Commons. I feel, as a layman and one who has some experience with the various types of mental illness, that this subject is not one upon which we need any national survey. I think anyone familiar with the subject knows how many people are suffering from the various types of mental illness as well as the treatments for those

types of mental illnesses. There are different types of treatments for these mental illnesses, and if they are successful in Canada they are successful in the United States; if they work in one province, then they work in another province. I do not see any need for research that is national in scope. What we want is research on the different mental illnesses. It is not a case of spending a lot of money on a lot of things. What we want to do is concentrate and push forward on certain subjects that are related to the various mental illnesses.
I feel that this is what the mover of the resolution had in mind. I am sure it is what some of the medical men had in mind when they spoke this afternoon. This debate on this subject has been very timely and many of the laymen in this house have learned a lot from listening to our medical confreres in this house. I am prepared, as I said, to support anything the government feels can be done in this regard. However, I feel our government should be guided by what the medical profession feels it can do, and the research that can be performed. I do not believe we should just say we will vote $10 million or $12 million, and see if you can use it. I think our minister is proceeding in this fashion, carefully looking into what research is required. We will certainly keep abreast of the requirements and do everything that is necessary to push forward this research. I think it was a grand thing for the hon. member for Mount Royal to bring this resolution forward in order that the views of the people across this country may be obtained on this important subject.

I should like to join with the hon. member for Vic-toria-Carleton (Mr. Montgomery) in his praise of the sponsor of this resolution. I think most of us will agree that mental illness, in all its ramifications and perplexities, is one of our greatest single domestic problems. As a practising lawyer I have some knowledge of the connection between mental illness and crime. I believe the Department of Justice is fully aware of the fact that in the treatment of criminals and those convicted of crime there must be some recognition given to the part played by mental illnesses.
Mental illnesses are difficult to treat because we are dealing with human beings, the relationship of human beings to one another and to their environment. Although man has made great strides in understanding the mental processes there are still areas which are baffling to the human mind. In order to give you some idea of the immensity of this problem I should like to say that at the end of 1957 Canada's mental hospitals, exclusive

of psychiatric units, were treating more than 72,000 patients. Despite the rate of discharges, the number of patients has increased each year. Since 1948, 14,000 mental beds have been added to our total.
Some provinces have separate hospitals in which the separate categories are treated. For instance, in the province of New Brunswick legislation was passed in 1958, authorizing the government to contribute to the maintenance of mentally retarded children kept in private homes. As a matter of fact, the largest provincial group of medical personnel in the province of New Brunswick is engaged in that work and I think this is true in most of the other provinces. As the method of treatment improves the patients are allowed more freedom. This is accomplished not only through an increase in knowledge but through the use of the newer drugs.
There is a great need also for the treatment of mentally defectives outside of institutions. This is being undertaken by associations. As the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton pointed out, I do not believe a national survey is necessary because the number of those who require treatment is well known. However, we do need additional funds and we do need additional trained personnel. The trained personnel are difficult to obtain because many people do not wish to engage in this work. I think the resolution for these reasons, and considering its impact on the many phases of our national life, should receive the support of all members in this house. I feel that any money contributed by this government, in addition to that supplied by the provincial governments, will be money well spent in a worthy cause.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. H. A. Thomas (Middlesex West):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very glad to associate myself with the other hon. members in this house who have endorsed this very worthy resolution put forward by the hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. Macnaughton). I am pleased indeed to note the changed attitude in recent years toward the people who suffer from mental disorders. No longer is this tribulation considered to arise from supernatural causes; no longer is it considered, as in olden days, a devil to be cast out by miraculous means. It is recognized to be the result of the malfunction of the glands of the body, the growth of tumours in the brain, trouble with the circulatory system or the result, in these modern times, of nervous tensions.
People who suffer from these troubles are no longer considered outcasts from society. They are regarded the same as anyone else who suffers from an illness of any kind. The 90205-6-34
Mental Illness Survey
stigma is being removed and our mental institutions, instead of being places where it is a shame to go, are recognized as the proper places to which people go for treatment of mental afflictions.
It was with great interest that last summer I went on a trip to St. Mary's hospital at Ste. Anne de Bellevue in Montreal with the standing committee on veterans affairs. We visited the psychiatric wards of that institution and were informed by the medical directors there that within the last two years, due to the introduction of new tranquillizer type treatments, it had been possible to remove the locks and bars from a number of corridors that used to be locked and barred. Instead of noise and confusion caused by patients suffering from mental torment, everything in the institution was calm and peaceful and all the patients seemed to be living a normal life.
If action by this house, as a result of the passage of this resolution, leads to improving these treatments and the whole handling of the treatment of mental troubles, then this house will have today performed a real service in the debate and processing of this resolution.
We are living in a changing world and the changes seem to have been connected largely with speed. Our civilization has become a speed-crazy civilization. We start our children off to school and they are urged from the beginning to make the best possible use of their time. Everything they do is measured in time. No class of our population is under greater pressure of work than our school children, especially teenagers in high school and later on in university.
When they pass through school they go out and take a job, and nearly everything they do is measured in terms of time. They can lay so many bricks per hour; they can earn so many cents per hour, or so many dollars per day or per week. The pressure of time seems to be connected with everything we do.
People today are suffering to a greater extent than ever before from social pressure resulting from this speed-crazy attitude which prevails in the western world. If the research which is proposed in this resolution can pinpoint our troubles in this connection and can do anything toward smoothing out the mental stress and strain from which our people suffer, then we will have accomplished something worthwhile. I am glad to support this resolution. I think it is very timely and could conceivably bring about a great improvement in the conditions under which we live.

Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to speak on this resolution. However, since so many members from both

Mental Illness Survey
sides of the house have spoken on the matter I, too, would like to extend to the hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. Macnaughton) my appreciation for his bringing this matter to the House of Commons.
A considerable amount of progress has been made in the riding which I represent in the manner of treating our retarded children and also caring for our mentally ill. I recall that it is only a few short years ago since retarded' children-who are to a great extent mentally ill-were kept indoors and were very seldom seen. Then a few people began to get little schools together for them. In those days there was no financial assistance from either the federal or provincial government for either the building of schools for retarded children or the provision of teachers.
However, conditions have changed in the last few years and all over this province, I am pleased to note, retarded children's schools are being built. I have watched the progress that has been made by some of these children, and I can assure you, gentlemen, that it is remarkable. I have followed some of them all the way through from the time they went to school and I have seen quite a number of them who were able to attend public schools and complete their education.
As far as the mentally ill are concerned, a few years ago the hon. member for Durham (Mr. Vivian) who spoke this afternoon was the minister of public health for the province of Ontario. We were building a large addition to our hospital, and he came to us and asked us to build a psychiatric wing. We were rather reluctant to do this at that time. However, due to his persuasion a 22-bed psychiatric wing was added to our hospital, and also a large outdoor clinic.
I can assure you that this has been one of the finest things we have done in the city of St. Catharines for the care of our mentally ill. It has been said in this house that those who were mentally ill were rather shunned and looked down upon. But today it is quite different, and those who go to hospital for care in connection with mental illness are looked upon just the same as other people who go into our hospitals for other types of treatment.
I can assure you, gentlemen, that this 22-bed hospital we built has not only served the needs of the people in our riding but it has also taken in patients from other parts of the province. At one time-as was the case in other parts of the province-there were quite a number of our people who had to go to mental institutions, and after they went in they were very seldom seen again. However, it is quite different today, because if mental illness is treated in its early stages and given the proper treatment it can be

cured in a great many cases. I myself have witnessed many cases where this has happened. So I am very happy at this time to support this resolution, which I am sure is going to receive the sympathetic consideration of this house. Again I extend to the sponsor my sincere congratulations. I think it is a step which will be well taken, and this resolution seems to be a very popular one in the house this evening.

The
mover of this resolution, the hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. Macnaughton) made a most impressive case for his motion and I feel that every member of this house is in sympathy with his remarks. Having heard various hon. members speak on the subject, the only observation I should like to make is that the resolution may be a little awkwardly worded. It says, and I quote:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of co-operating with the provincial authorities and such professional and other groups as may be interested, in making a national survey of the extent of mental illness, its causes, problems and method of treatment.
This is one of those national problems which affect all Canadians. It is not limited by provincial boundaries. It is one of those problems which need leadership, and I suggest, with all due respect to the hon. member for Mount Royal who, as I say, made a magnificent case for his motion, that perhaps this national effort should have as its initiator the national government; that the provincial governments should be asked to cooperate with this government, this house and this parliament, and that the other bodies, with their technical skills, the medical schools, the hospitals with their records of cases far beyond our comprehension, should be asked to sit down with the major body in Ottawa to devise a plan which would be effective in the next few years.
Can we proceed without the other entities?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Monleiih (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I too, would like to compliment the hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. Macnaughton) for presenting this resolution today. I believe he had a similar resolution on the order paper last year but there was no opportunity to discuss it. I am very happy that we are now in a position to consider his motion. Indeed, I should like to congratulate all hon. members who have taken part in the discussion. I am very happy to have the benefit of their views and comments on the subject; they will be well worth-while in dealing with the whole question.

The subject which we have discussed in connection with this resolution has, I think, demonstrated a degree of agreement which is somewhat unusual, and I suggest, as did the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin), that it crosses party lines. I should like in particular to congratulate the hon. member for Mount Royal on the content of his speech on moving the resolution. I do not want to be political, but he did suggest that there might be more efficient use made of the money available for health purposes and that this government should show more initiative and devote more study to this problem. I should just like to say that I do not think we should completely discount what has already been done by this government.
This whole debate has been on a very high plane and I should like to keep it there, but perhaps hon. members will permit me to read a few remarks from the brief presented by the Canadian Mental Health Association to the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) and members of the cabinet as of Friday last. Part of the brief reads as follows:
At the beginning, we wish to express our pleasure in the constructive and helpful attitude we have found among individual members of this government and of parliament whenever the nation's mental health problems have been considered at federal level. We have noted with satisfaction that the personal interest of many members of parliament is shown in the active memberships they hold in one or another of our 120 local branches across Canada. But beyond this, we have marked with gratification the ways in which progressively larger amounts of federal funds are being directed into mental health work. We experienced some of the impact of this when the federal grant to the Canadian Mental Health Association was increased in 1958 from $10,000 to $15,000, after remaining static for some 22 years. Furthermore, though still not adequate to meet the urgent developing needs in the field, we must recognize that current federal appropriations for mental health work are at a higher level than ever before. This concrete evidence of interest in mental health by the present parliament of Canada encourages us to appear today with confidence that the views we express wiil receive sympathetic consideration.
That, by the way, was released as of ten o'clock on December 2, 1960.
As one who shares the concern of the hon. member for Mount Royal, as one who shares his opinion and who also believes that public understanding of mental illness is of vital importance, I welcome wholeheartedly the hon. member's initiative. From the tone of the resolution it is obvious that it involves a constructive effort to explore and clarify one of our top health problems in a spirit of objective and earnest inquiry. I intend to deal with the resolution in some detail, but before doing so there are some general comments I should like to make on the problem of mental illness in Canada and what is currently being done about it. I believe that what I have to say on the 90205-6-341
Mental Illness Survey
resolution will be more informative when viewed in the perspective of our past and present endeavours.
I have said that mental illness is one of Canada's top health problems. I do not intend to repeat all the statistics which have been given today by various members. They were all most helpful and indicative of the problem. Incidentally, the hon. member for Mount Royal gave a quotation from a speech I made in Stratford. He mentioned that I said there were approximately 75,000 Canadians in the care of mental hospitals and other mental health facilities. This is so, but if I may correct the hon. member on one small detail, he spoke of "the town of Stratford". Since this is my own constituency, I should like the hon. member to know that Stratford is a city, and whenever I get the opportunity I like, of course, to mention the Stratford Shakespearean Festival.
There are these 74,000 people, roughly, in the care of mental hospitals. We also have psychiatric units in general hospitals, and these must also be taken into account. Indications are that they may be treating an additional 1,000 patients. There are mental health clinics for which no accurate figures are available, and over and above all of this are persons with varying degrees of mental illness who are not reported as receiving treatment. The situation therefore becomes somewhat more blurred and uncertain as you move away from the hard core of readily identifiable mental illness. Indeed, a very real problem is that of defining precisely what is mental illness.
Opinions differ widely. A recent study in Ontario suggests that one out of every 15 Canadians will spend part of his life in mental hospitals of one kind or another. Other authorities have thrown the net wider and maintained that a large proportion of people seen by their family doctors suffer from some degree of emotional disability. If there is uncertainty about the extent of mental illness there is equal doubt about whether or not it is on the increase.
A study of admission rates to mental hospitals in Canada covering the period 1946 to 1956 indicated an increase of 117 per cent. But, this may not be too meaningful. It does not take into account such factors as increased facilities for statement and the changing public attitude toward mental illness which has encouraged more and more patients to seek early and adequate treatment. In view of this and other considerations the consensus appears to be that while the problem of mental illness is substantial-

Mental Illness Survey
it has been termed the largest special medical and hospital problem in Canada today actually-its exact dimensions are not yet clearly defined.
Having noted the seriousness of the problem I would go on to say that prospects for progress in the field of mental illness are more hopeful today than ever before. I think this optimistic outlook is very firmly based. It arises chiefly from what has been called the quiet revolution that has gradually occurred throughout all aspects of the problem. In a phrase, this represents a shift from the negative to the positive. Instead of regarding it as outside the course of normal human experience we are coming to look upon mental illness as a disease like any other to which human beings are susceptible. Rather than submitting patients to long term commitments in mental hospitals where they are isolated from their home and community it is being increasingly accepted that hospitalization should only be an incident in the patient's illness. This illness begins long before hospitalization and does not end when the patient returns to his regular environment.
Scientific advances have, of course, played a leading role in bringing about these shifts. The development and use of tranquillizers- as has been mentioned frequently here today -and other drugs have made possible a much stronger emphasis on treatment. They have, in fact, almost revolutionized the treatment of many types of mental disorder. Someone has even compared their development to the discovery of anaesthetics in making possible the treatment of patients who would otherwise be inaccessible to therapy.
While other factors no doubt are also involved, I think it is evident that tranquillizers and similar drugs can take much credit for the substantial decline in average length of stay in mental hospitals. In 1947 this amounted to 1.3 years; in 1957, it had dropped to 5 months. This new approach to mental illness through chemotherapy was initiated in Europe but Canadians can be proud of the fact that our scientists have made vital contributions to its introduction in mental hospital practice.
As the house may recall, Dr. Heinz Lehmann, clinical director of the Verdun Protestant hospital, won a Lasker award several years ago for his work in this field. In addition to chemotherapy, an important factor in recent progress has been the growing emphasis on the so-called open door policy in mental hospitals. While this is still at an early stage of development, experience so far holds out great hope for its therapeutic value. I imagine that the phrase "open door" is self-explanatory and I would only add that

its aim is to reverse the feeling of being caged in which has often been a major obstacle to successful treatment and recovery.
Another indication of the shift toward treatment is the development of psychiatric units in general hospitals. There are now over 40 units in Canada as against less than 10 a dozen years ago. In 1958 almost a third of all mental patient first admissions and readmissions were to these units. I would not imply that psychiatric units in general hospitals are replacing mental hospitals but I do think that their use represents a growing tendency to treat acute mental disorders within the mainstream of community health services.
If treatment is on the upswing in mental illness so also is rehabilitation which incidentally is where the shift to community-based programs becomes apparent. More and more it is being recognized that rehabilitation should commence as early as possible in the history of the illness and should constitute a continuing and integral part of the treatment program. It should also be maintained after the patient returns home. This inevitably involves broad and active support on the part of the community. Although much remains to be done, community participation is growing and is taking such forms as the provision of clubs, foster homes and other services designed to re-establish the patient in society.
Community mental health clinics are also playing an increasing role in rehabilitation but their greatest contribution is in another area. This is in keeping patients out of hospitals, keeping them on the job and active at home and in their neighbourhood. This is not only beneficial to the patient's recovery but also to the economic position of his family. A recent innovation in this regard is the day and night centre in which Canada has been an outstanding pioneer. Indeed, we have won world-wide recognition for centres like those established in Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver which provide treatment on a nine to five basis or in the evening after working hours.
Mental health services for children have also been widely developed in the past few years. For example, there are special children's wards in certain of our general hospitals as well as a fair number of residential treatment centres in various communities across the country.
The problem of mental retardation has been tackled to an extensive degree. Hundreds of community day schools supported by parent groups and designed especially for the trainable retarded child have sprung up throughout Canada. Provincial training schools have also been improved and the advantages of

sheltered work shops for older youngsters explored. These are some of the advances which have helped transform the whole field of mental illness. They have been bolstered and in many cases made possible by the increasing interest and support of voluntary agencies, professional groups and governments at all levels. The voluntary aspect, I believe, is particularly encouraging.
I have already spoken of the growing trend toward community responsibility. This has been sparked to a large extent by the activities of organizations like the Canadian Mental Health Association, the Canadian Association for Retarded Children and numerous local groups working in the field of rehabilitation and on behalf of emotionally disturbed children.
I should just like to read a very few brief remarks concerning the Canadian Mental Health Association to show the house what it has been doing. It dates from 1918, but the structure of the national office, provincial divisions and community branches was set up in 1950. The national office controls nine provincial divisions comprising 90 branches and a membership of 115,000. I think this is explanatory of the worth-whileness of this organization.
I mentioned, Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Association for Retarded Children. I should like to point out that in a letter written to me recently they say this:
These expressions of your department's keen interest in and appreciation of the effective part which the Canadian Association for Retarded Children is taking in the field of mental retardation "have assisted materially toward attainment of the general objectives stated in the above cited brief''.
I should like to read objectives (a) and (b):
(a)	To assist its affiliated associations and other agencies to improve the welfare of mentally retarded persons and their families, wherever they may be in Canada, and
(b)	To stimulate programs in the fields of mental and clinical research with the object of seeking means to prevent the occurrence of mental retardation.
To me these are very worth-while and constructive efforts. I think, Mr. Speaker, public education is also a vital part of these voluntary efforts, and some indication of how this is paying off can be seen in the increasing proportion of voluntary admissions to mental treatment facilities. In the case of psychiatric units in general hospitals, this rose in 1957 to a full 99 per cent.
As far as government is concerned, the provinces have traditionally accepted primary responsibility for mental hospitals and mental treatment generally. In recent years, however, the dominion government has increasingly entered the picture by providing
Mental Illness Survey
financial and technical assistance to provincial programs. I think, for instance, of the national health grants, one of the largest of which was set aside for mental health purposes.
As was mentioned this afternoon, we started in 1948 with a mental health grant of $4 million a year. Today it is more than double that amount, totalling $8.7 million. This figure is more than $1.5 million higher than the allocation for last year, when the mental health grant was pegged at just over $7.2 million. This increase was decided upon after consultation with the provinces.
It was pointed out earlier that over the 12-year period $54.5 million was spent. This tremendous amount has had a real impact. About half of it has gone to support services in mental hospitals which, as I mentioned, have been the traditional responsibility of the provinces. Now, thanks to this joint effort, less than 10 per cent of the cost of mental hospital operations has to be met by patients and their families.
Another area in which the mental health grant has been important is in stimulating the development of psychiatriac units in general hospitals. I have already referred to these units as part of the new look in mental health. Equally impressive has been the stimulus to the creation of a widespread network of community health centres. In 1948 these clinics numbered fewer than 20. Today the number has risen to nearly 150, more than half of which are attached to out-patient departments of general hospitals.
The mental health grant has also had a strong impact on research, which has been discussed at some length here today. The number of projects receiving support has risen from 13 in 1949-50 to over 60 last year with federal expenditures for the period amounting to over $4.5 million. This year, mental health grants support for research has been increased to over $800,000 as against $750,000 in 1959-60.
To give the house an idea of the kind of work which is being carried on with federal support I should like to list a few of the projects currently in the program: A study of protein metabolism and its relation to psychiatric states and their treatment; a study of the function of the hormones of the brain; an investigation of the relation of personality and somatic factors to cholesterol metabolism; endocrine and metabolic aspects of mental deficiency; a study of methods of evaluation and mechanisms of the action of tranquillizers; the post-discharge adaptation of psychiatric patients to the community. These are all very worth-while research program which are going on. Some of this type of effort has been discussed this afternoon.

Mental Illness Survey
The mental health grant has also contributed to the training of expert personnel. Thanks to bursaries provided through the grants program some 2,600 professional and technical workers have received training in various specialties. I hardly need remind the house of the necessity for adequate staff to the operation and development of mental health services. Federal support through the health grants has made a contribution to the expansion of mental hospitals in Canada.
Since 1948 the hospital construction grant has provided over $29 million toward the construction of over 20,000 new beds in mental hospitals. Finally, mental health services have received a new impetus through the hospital insurance and diagnostic services program which covers the operation of psychiatric units in general hospitals.
With this background in mind, Mr. Speaker, I should like to turn again to the resolution now before the house in the name of the hon. member for Mount Royal. As I said before, I feel that this can best be evaluated against the pattern of our mental health structure and progress. From what I have said regarding our lack of knowledge about the nature and extent of mental illness in Canada, it will be evident that I myself and officials of my department welcome any suggestion or step which might lead to a greater understanding in this respect. This being so, I can say that I wholeheartedly agree with the spirit of this resolution. There is no doubt that it is highly constructive in its over-all objective. I will go even further and say it merits renewed consideration and to this end I propose to ask my officials to have it placed on the agenda of the forthcoming meeting of my advisory committee on mental health.
I might explain that this committee is a key factor in Canada's mental health program, comprising as it does representatives of my department, provincial directors of mental health, university representation from the professions of psychiatry, psychology and social work as well as a representative of the Canadian psychiatric association and the Canadian Mental Health Association. This is the basic vehicle for the close cooperation between the provinces, the dominion government and professional and voluntary groups on which our whole effort is founded.
Having said that, I feel that I should point out that the idea of a national survey as proposed by the hon. member has not been overlooked in our considerations. It has been the subject of a good deal of discussion during which certain points have been raised which I believe must be taken into account. Let me mention a few.

While the idea of a survey of the prevalence of mental illness in Canada is regarded as a sound one, certain difficulties become apparent when one approaches its actual implementation. The first I have already mentioned, the problem of defining mental illness. Do you include only patients in mental hospitals or do you throw the net wider to cover psychiatric units in general hospitals as well as mental health clinics? Even if this broader concept is adopted, what do you do about cases of mental illness abroad in the community which are not being treated? This latter group presumably would be very difficult to assess and yet if it were not included would we have a reasonable picture of the problem? Thanks to the continuing efforts of the dominion bureau of statistics we already have figures for mental hospitals and psychiatric units. Noting the difficulties I have mentioned regarding cases not under treatment, would a national survey really add a great deal to our present knowledge?
In addition to this difficulty, there is the fact that a survey as suggested by the hon. member would be a very complex procedure involving the development of adequate sampling arrangements, the training of interviewers, the working out of effective question-aires and so on. Because of these problems it would also be a very expensive undertaking. For example, a survey of the type suggested has recently been carried out in one county of one of the provinces and while it did produce some very useful data it cost upwards of $150,000. I repeat that it cost upwards of $150,000 and it covered only one county.
The hon. member for Essex East referred earlier to some surveys and he mentioned the one in 1948. Actually there had been an amount of money expended by way of a planning and organization grant for the introduction of health insurance back in 1945 and it was eventually switched to a health survey grant to the provinces to survey health and hospital needs at the time of the health grants. This survey was completed in the period from 1949 to 1951. The provinces prepared their own reports of programs and services, hospital beds required and so on. This information was required for the introduction of the national health grants at that time. The term "extent" and the involvement of the term "extent" was not included in the survey.
A few years later there was another survey by our department and the provinces in conjunction with the bureau of statistics but here again the emphasis was on physical illness and not mental. Actually the early results of the last survey I mentioned have

been out for some little time in the consolidation of the interim bulletin which was produced earlier this year. This does not adequately cover the mental field.
The survey in one county of one province to which I referred also highlighted the implications of the first problem I mentioned, namely what should be included in a definition of mental illness. Taking only mental and general hospitals this survey came up with an incidence of 47 per one thousand population. Taking known hospital cases plus other cases located through actual sampling of the population and physicians' reports, it produced an incidence of 370 per one thousand population. This is quite a gap and it points to the degree of error that might develop unless an over-all standard was rigidly enforced. This in itself would be extremely difficult having in mind the great differences in social organization across the country.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, such a survey would involve a large number of trained personnel and would, therefore, tie up a good portion of our mental health staff for a considerable period. This point was mentioned this afternoon. These are some of the factors which have led officials of my department, their colleagues in the provinces and in voluntary and professional organizations not to reject a national survey out of hand but rather to recommend a more selective approach under present circumstances.
At the moment, for example, three particular areas are receiving special attention. These are psychiatric units in general hospitals, in-patient services for mentally disturbed children and the open door approach in mental institutions. In the past other areas have come in for particular study. These include after-care services for discharged patients and personnel needs. This selective approach has proved highly effective and the consensus among mental health experts has been for its continuation.
There are various pamphlets published both by my department and the dominion bureau of statistics. The bureau of statistics has accumulated a vast amount of data which appeared in "Mental Health Statistics" published in 1958. My department has also produced "Mental Health Services in Canada" which was first published in 1954 and is currently being brought up to date.
Another point I might mention has to do with a development now under way in British Columbia. At the request of the provincial government a survey is being carried out of provincial mental health needs and resources. This work is still in progress and as yet no findings have been made available.
Business of the House
As far as the causes of mental illness are concerned, these of course are matters for research, and I have already mentioned this field. I hope that these comments will not be interpreted as being too negative or as an effort to throw cold water on the suggestion put forward by the hon. member for Mount Royal. This is certainly not my intention. At the same time I have felt I should be frank with the hon. member and with the house in pointing out some of the problems which have been raised in this connection in the past and which may well still be considered decisive. Be that as it may, I welcome the opportunity which this resolution has afforded the house for a discussion of this very important health problem. Personally I believe that the more responsible discussion and consideration which is given to the matter of mental illness the better chances will be for future progress which is, of course, our common objective. I therefore want to commend the hon. member for Mount Royal again for taking this initiative.
It would seem, Mr. Speaker, that all who wish to speak on this resolution have spoken. At least, it appeared that way when I rose to my feet. I should like to say that the government accepts this motion in principle realizing that much further examination, in the light of some of the difficulties and problems I have mentioned, must be given to the project before it can actually be undertaken.
Motion agreed to.

Mr. Speaker, having regard to the hour, perhaps the house would agree to calling it ten o'clock. On Friday night the leader of the house for the government indicated that he would be a little more expansive in indicating the work of the house for this week. Perhaps he would now give the house more information in that regard.

I expressed the hope on Friday night but I have not much more information. Tomorrow we will proceed with the resolution in the name of the Minister of Labour dealing with technical and vocational training. If the resolution passes quickly, and we have had quite an extensive debate on it, it will be open to the house to proceed with the other stages of the bill. That can be decided when the time arises. That resolution would be followed by the one standing in the name of the Minister of Trade and Commerce dealing with the productivity council proposal. If that is completed and time permits we would consider the setting up of the four special committees for this

Business of the House year, the one on procedure, followed by the one on Indian affairs, then research and then broadcasting.
For Wednesday there would be the second reading, if not complete, of the bill based on the resolution concerning technical and vocational training, and the second reading of the bill dealing with the productivity council. Thursday will be private member's day. The business for Friday I will endeavour to

give the house tomorrow, depending on the progress we make with the matters I have outlined.
